Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.

title: Astropad Workbench 1.4 adds terminal access, iPhone Duo support, and more
snippet: Astropad is out today with Workbench 1.4, the latest update to its remote desktop app for Mac. The release adds a built-in terminal, native iPhone Duo support, and a new way to transfer files between Macs. more…
fullText:
Astropad is out today with Workbench 1.4, the latest update to its remote desktop app for Mac. The release adds a built-in terminal, native iPhone Duo support, and a new way to transfer files between Macs.

Workbench first launched in April with a focus on accessing your Mac from an iPhone or iPad, including checking on AI agents while away from your desk. Version 1.3 arrived in August with faster streaming, a privacy curtain, picture-in-picture support, and tools for keeping unattended Macs accessible.

The big addition in Workbench 1.4 is the ability to switch between the remote desktop and terminal without reconnecting. A toolbar control lets users move between Screen and Terminal views. On Mac, the terminal opens in a separate window.

That means you can check logs, edit a script, or restart a process without opening a separate SSH app. Terminal sessions also keep running between connections, so you can start on an iPad and return later from an iPhone or another Mac.

Voice input works with the terminal as well, letting users dictate prompts and commands. For Mac-to-Mac connections, Workbench now supports dragging and dropping files during terminal sessions.

Astropad says the update also runs natively on iPhone Duo, with support for keeping an agent visible in one pane while using the rest of the phone.

Workbench remains free for 20 minutes of access per day. Unlimited access is currently priced at $14.99/month or $79.99/year. The app requires macOS 15 or later, iOS 26 or later, or iPadOS 26 or later.

title: Opera One now lets Mac users run Apple’s foundation model directly in the browser
snippet: Starting today, Opera One users can access a preview feature that lets them tap into local AI models through WebAI, a proposed web standard. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Starting today, Opera One users can access a preview feature that lets them tap into local AI models through WebAI, a proposed web standard. Here are the details.

WebAI

Opera announced today that its Opera One browser is the first of its browsers to offer built-in access to local AI models, with Opera GX and Opera Neon to follow.

The feature relies on the WebAI proposed web standard, which allows websites and browser extensions to access AI models running locally on the user’s device.

Here’s Opera:

WebAI is a proposed web standard, backed by companies such as Google and Microsoft, that lets websites and browser extensions use AI hosted through the browser. Opera’s implementation is model-agnostic and built around open models, offering users choice among AI providers. At launch, users can already tap into models from Google and Apple, including Google’s Gemma and, on Macs, Apple’s on-device foundation model, directly in Opera.

The company notes that WebAI can be used to generate text, classify content, and identify relationships between pieces of information, and adds that the feature is opt-in, with no subscription needed, and with users able to control which websites can access local AI models.

Here’s Opera again on some of the potential uses for local AI in the browser:

With local AI built into the browser, both users and developers can benefit from new capabilities. Local AI lets anyone build on top of free, open-weight AI models. Developers can add AI features without running AI infrastructure or paying for every request. Users don’t need AI subscriptions, the information the local AI handles stays on their own device, and they stay in control of the AI on their computer. For example, an extension could sort your tabs, flag clickbait or spot relevant job posts using a model on your laptop, with no account, no fee and no data sent to an AI service.

To help developers (and users) explore what’s possible with WebAI, Opera has released a collection of example extensions that you can find here.

HTML-in-Canvas

Additionally, Opera is launching HTML-in-Canvas today, which, as the company explains, “lets developers put real, interactive web pages inside 2D and 3D scenes.”

The feature allows developers to embed fully functional web pages into 2D and 3D environments, with interactive elements such as menus, buttons, and forms remaining usable even as they move around within a scene. Developers can build these experiences using familiar HTML and CSS.

Here’s Maciej Kocemba, Product Director at Opera GX:

“Honestly, this is a fun one […]. You can take a real web page and throw it into a 3D world, and everything still works: buttons, text, menus, all of it. We wanted users to get their hands on it early and see what they come up with.”

To demonstrate the possibilities, Opera has created two examples: Webpage Bulldozer, which turns elements of a web page into physical objects, and Gamer Room, a virtual 3D room featuring screens that display live web pages. Both demos work in Opera browsers without any additional setup, and you can check them out ⁠here.

title: Using AI to Vibe Code Your TV Is Stupid
snippet: No one likes clunky TV interfaces or their activity being tracked, but using AI isn’t how to avoid it. There’s an easier way.
fullText:
Recently, some posts on X/Twitter and discussed elsewhere have claimed that AI has helped people “vibe code” their way to a better TV interface. Less clutter, no ads, less tracking and more are all ascribed to AI’s magical powers. Not only is this nonsense, but it’s also stupid. 

First, let me say up front that I understand the frustration. TV interfaces have gotten bloated; they often have ads, and their creepy and invasive tracking properties have long been discussed and warned about by me and others. 

That said, AI is not doing anything unique here. Not only can you do this without AI, but it’s also probably better if you don’t. Using AI risks potentially TV-ruining issues or worse.

			

More from CNET

What’s happening

“Vibe coding” is the colloquial term for using AI to assist or fully write programming code for apps, websites and so on. Instead of learning a programming language, people tell AI agents in plain English (or their language of choice) what they want, and the AI does it, or at least something close to it. 

In this case, people are claiming they’re using an AI agent, usually Claude, to write a new operating system for TVs. This “new” OS is, they claim, faster, easier to use, has no ads and so on.

Why it’s a bad idea 

As with all claims about AI, you should be suspicious. First, TV operating systems are far more complex than they appear. Messing around “under the hood,” especially with no programming knowledge, can easily cause serious problems.

One TV engineer I spoke to for this article, who asked to remain anonymous, literally laughed out loud when I asked him about this. He explained that his engineers will often fix one bug in their software, and it will cause 10 other bugs in random, seemingly unrelated parts of the TV. That’s pretty typical with software development, by the way. There are reports already that people have “bricked” their TVs trying this. As in, they turned their TV into an expensive and unusable brick.

The Google TV interface on a Sony Bravia 9 II.Ty Pendlebury/CNET

There are also a lot of potential issues down the road, even if you have initial success. For instance, will the new vibe-coded OS actually run Netflix and other apps? They might seem to load and then not be able to play anything. What happens if one of the apps needs an update? Will you still be able to? What if that update requires a specific Android version? Maybe you won’t have any issues, but there’s no guarantee of that, and if you don’t have any background in software or coding, can you be sure that more AI vibe coding will fix the issue? Will you be able to perform a factory reset and restore it to the way it was when you bought it? Hopefully yes, but not necessarily.

If you’re not a programmer, how sure are you that the code you’re using is secure? How sure are you that it’s only doing what you want and not exposing your TV to external access? This isn’t as likely as just breaking your TV, but if you don’t know or understand what’s going on “under the hood,” can you really be sure?

And what’s the end goal here? If it’s a faster interface with fewer ads, you can do that already without AI, as I’ll discuss in the next section. If it’s to minimize tracking, maybe changing the OS or interface will help, but not entirely.

Why it’s really stupid: An easier solution already exists

AI can’t invent anything, and you can already change your TV’s interface with just an app install. Android TV launchers, as in the user interface, can be swapped out. So if your TV runs on Android, you can change the interface without any AI vibe coding. These launchers are often far simpler than the stock Google TV interface and are highly customizable. 

Projectivy Launcher

Launchers like Projectivity, Monet and TV Launcher Premium Smart UI are some of the top-rated and most popular ones. The AT4K Launcher even makes your Android TV interface look like the Apple TV interface. There are many more options.

If you have a TV with a company-specific operating system, like LG’s webOS, Samsung’s Tizen, Hisense’s VIDAA and so on, the AI vibe coding trick isn’t likely to work anyway. Companies do their best to lock down their operating systems to prevent exactly the kind of thing we’re talking about here. 

Monet Launcher

It’s entirely arguable that AI wasn’t doing anything clever in the first place. It was just regurgitating what human programmers had already figured out.

What you can do instead

I think there’s a hilarious irony in not wanting your personal data to be out there, so in order to block your TV from tracking you, you give your personal data to AI. If you don’t understand why that’s ironic, you definitely shouldn’t give your data to AI. As I’ve talked about before, there is no easy way to prevent your TV from tracking you and selling your data. You can minimize it, or go to more extreme measures like Pi-holes and not connecting it to the internet at all, but then you’ll just be switching which device is tracking you. Still want streaming? All the streaming devices track you to some extent (the Apple TV 4K less so). 

AT4K Launcher

Using AI to vibe code your way into a better TV experience, however, is a dumb idea. Try a launcher app first and see if that gets you most or all the way to what you’re looking for. Will it be a magical fix to speed up a slow TV? No, but it could be much closer to what you’re looking for, and it’s far less likely to nuke your TV. If you want to go even further, there are apps that give you even more control, but with more potential for issues. Or hey, if you have a TV you don’t mind ruining, and you want to see what you can come up with using an AI that is just stealing from other people’s work, go for it.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Geoffrey Morrison
						

						

							Contributor

He is the author of Budget Travel for Dummies as well as the bestselling sci-fi novels Undersea, and Undersea Atrophia. title: iPhone Duo could capture nearly 30% of foldable market in 2027, per report
snippet: In a report released today, TrendForce says that with strong demand for the iPhone Duo out of the gate, Apple is poised to capture nearly 30% of the global foldable smartphone market by 2027. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a report released today, TrendForce says that with strong demand for the iPhone Duo out of the gate, Apple is poised to capture nearly 30% of the global foldable smartphone market by 2027. Here are the details.

One day after Apple announced the iPhone Duo last month, TrendForce published a report predicting that the company would ship 5 million units of its first foldable iPhone by the end of 2026, capturing 24.8% of the segment.

At the time, TrendForce expected the overall foldable smartphone market to grow by just 0.5% in 2026, with shipments from Android brands alone falling by more than 20% year over year.

By contrast, TrendForce expected the market to reach 23.5 million shipments in 2027, a 16.3% increase. The firm also suggested that Apple’s entry could help drive future growth through improvements in foldable technology, while new AI use cases could further boost demand.

With the iPhone Duo now shipping for nearly a week, TrendForce published a new report today reiterating its previous projections and forecasting that Apple will capture 29.8% of the foldable smartphone market in 2027.

	

From the report:

TrendForce notes that Apple’s greatest advantage lies in its ability to integrate chips, operating systems, and its developer ecosystem. As app compatibility and hardware reliability improve, the Duo is expected to further expand the practical value of foldable displays, helping shift competition in the foldable smartphone market from form-factor innovation toward multitasking efficiency.

If TrendForce’s projections pan out, Apple will hold second place in the foldable smartphone market in 2027, behind Samsung, whose share is expected to fall from 35.1% in 2026 to 31.9% next year, and ahead of Huawei, which is projected to drop from 24.8% to 21.3%.

title: The Massive DHS Breach Is Hacktivist Payback for Government Surveillance
snippet: The personal information of more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees was exposed by a hacker group.
fullText:
A Department of Homeland Security breach by an activist group has exposed the personal information of more than 41,000 employees, including Customs and Border Protection workers, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers and others who work in government cybersecurity.

Information collected from the breach was published online in a searchable repository called Icepick on the Distributed Denial of Secrets website. According to the news leaks site, a hacktivist group called the Department of Peace breached an Okta single sign-on service used by the DHS, stealing employees’ names, contact information and assignments. The group then distributed copies of the database through the leak-hosting group DDoSecrets and to a self-described investigative journalist and cybersecurity researcher from Switzerland known as maia arson crimew, who created an online tool to search the data.

The hacktivist crimew described the leak as an “unprecedented” and “massive” exposure of the DHS’s internal structure. By detailing exact roles, chains of command and agent identities across agencies like ICE, the dataset is a “complete game changer” that leaves the department highly vulnerable to outside investigation for years to come.

			

More from CNET

The breach appears to be the latest retaliation against government-led surveillance, including ICE’s increasingly tech-driven enforcement tactics and private partnerships with companies such as Flock Security. The Department of Peace directly cited DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s July statement about “turning up the heat on the streets” — a reference to ramping up the immigration crackdown and arrests — and responded, “This is what happens to ICE when you do that.” The hackers also attached a note to the files reading, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”

A DHS spokesperson told CNET that the agency “is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” The statement went on to say: “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.”

A massive leak of information 

Since the leak, the DHS has been working to take down sites hosting the information, including Icepick’s searchable archive domain. The social network Bluesky opted to block links to DDoSecrets, telling TechCrunch that the platform’s community guidelines prohibit “the unauthorized sharing of personal information and other content that could pose safety risks.”

Much of the attention on the Icepick leak has focused on its size. While the 41,000 affected employees represent only a fraction of the nearly quarter-million people at the DHS, the data goes far beyond basic contact information. Reports indicate the leak exposes office addresses and phone numbers, as well as details on internal work systems and the department’s inner workings.

Because the hackers gained access through Okta, a secure portal for employee login, they also saw the master list of apps connected to that dashboard. That revealed an inventory of surveillance applications used by ICE, including specialized wiretapping and surveillance software, such as Penlink, and popular AI applications like ChatGPT and Gemini, raising questions about how federal agencies feed case files or border data into commercial AI models. 

While cross-referencing Icepick data could expose undercover operations, it also risks including unrelated personnel, such as airport security workers. However, DDoSecrets cofounder and journalist Emma Best argued the release is strategic rather than an indiscriminate dump. “Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” Best wrote.

Retaliation against federal agencies

The public response to the breach also points to a crisis of institutional legitimacy, with many viewing the exposure not as a crime but as forced transparency against a federal department that has acted with impunity. In a Facebook comment thread accompanying an NPR story about the incident, many responded with support for the hacktivists: “Not all heroes wear capes,” one commenter wrote, while another said, “Law enforcement identities must be public. Otherwise, it’s just a gang.”

When an agency known for aggressive enforcement and widespread surveillance gets breached, a segment of the population sees it as poetic justice.

There’s also been an escalating operational crisis for any tech company that signs a contract with ICE or DHS agencies. From the outside, hacktivists are targeting their infrastructure (like this recent breach) to unmask federal agents and leak their surveillance toolkits. And from the inside, employees are sounding the alarm, demanding that leadership cancel contracts on moral grounds.

That was the case recently with the robot company Boston Dynamics, after it was reported that ICE planned to spend up to $2 million on Spot robots made by the company. Hundreds of employees signed a petition saying that they can’t be proud working for Boston Dynamics “when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians.” The employee noted that friends and family are asking them “in disbelief and horror” how they can work on ICE robots, an indication of broader distrust. 

The recent massive DHS breach isn’t a random, isolated cyberattack. Earlier this year, the Electronic Frontier Foundation detailed the spread of “enterprising hackers [that] have started projects to do counter surveillance against ICE,” including applications and web tools geared toward tracking officers’ movements and countering Flock surveillance cameras that can read license plates.

“It’s important to remember that we are not powerless,” wrote EFF’s Senior Staff Technologist Cooper Quintin. “Even in the face of a domestic law enforcement presence with massive surveillance capabilities and military-esque technologies, there are still ways to engage in surveillance self-defense.”

He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: AO3 Suffers Major Outage: Possibly No Fanfic for 2 Weeks or Longer
snippet: Archive of Our Own, one of the world’s biggest fanfiction sites, went down hard as a response to a “security incident.”
fullText:
October has been a rocky month for readers of the fan-run fiction site Archive of Our Own, popularly known as AO3. Now, a routine disruption has escalated into a crisis. What began as an estimated 12-hour unplanned outage has ballooned into a multi-week shutdown, leaving millions of users locked out of the site following a series of intermittent disruptions throughout the month.  An outage of this magnitude hit readers out of nowhere, landing with all the subtlety of a Looney Tunes anvil.

The platform is operated by the Organization for Transformative Works. An update posted Thursday to the site’s status page and shared via Bluesky and Tumblr said that service restoration will take at least two weeks, possibly four. 

“We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner,” the update said. “If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved.”

			

More from CNET

That update followed an initial notification, 12 hours earlier, with the announcement that “AO3 maintenance is in progress. We expect it to take at least 12 hours, but it may take longer.”

In response to a CNET request for more information, an OTW representative pointed to a new status update, saying, “The statement confirms that the downtime is a security incident, the scope of which is still being assessed. I can let you know that this is not related to the PHP security issue as the Archive uses Ruby on Rails.”

According to the update, “Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been found so far.”

It emphasizes that no data has been deleted, and while they don’t think user data was compromised, they can’t rule it out and recommend you change your password if it’s not unique to AO3. (It should be if you practice safe password practices.) Donor information resides in a separate, unconnected database.

If you need a stopgap for your fanfic needs, you can try Wattpad or FanFiction.  The r/DeletedFanfiction Reddit, Bluesky members and other communities have stepped up to offer copies of works they’d already downloaded and to crowdsource alternatives.

title: North Korean hackers blamed for stealing record $6.3B in Binance breach
snippet: Hackers working for North Korea are suspected of hacking a Binance employee's laptop, which allowed the theft of billions in crypto.
fullText:
Hackers working for the North Korean regime have been blamed for a record cryptocurrency heist following a cyberattack at crypto exchange Binance. The hackers stole at least $6.3 billion in crypto from the company’s wallets, though about half of that amount was frozen as the stolen crypto traveled across various blockchains, according to security researchers.

The breach is by far the largest known theft of crypto in history, though the incident has not been confirmed yet to be resolved, and the amount of crypto stolen may change.

In a post on X, Binance said its initial investigation showed that the hackers broke into the company’s network after targeting a “compromised” Binance engineer’s laptop, which “allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”

Binance said it has seen no evidence of a leak of its private keys, which would grant the hacker near-unfettered control over the company’s stores of crypto.

The crypto exchange — the world’s largest — said it has now suspended all deposits and withdrawals while its investigation into the breach continues. TechCrunch reported on Thursday that the exchange had paused withdrawals across some of its blockchains. 

Binance said “user funds are safe,” but did not immediately provide proof of this claim. The company said it will “publish an updated proof of reserves once the remediation is complete.”

Spokesperson Andie Cooper said in a statement shared with TechCrunch on Friday that some $3 billion has been frozen by industry partners. The spokesperson said Binance has “begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.” 

It’s unclear how the hack went down or under what circumstances the employee’s laptop was compromised, but it’s not uncommon for security incidents to stem from the use of compromised software on employee devices. 

Software is generally built from many components, including open-source projects, which hackers regularly target, compromise and modify in order to steal data from devices that the affected software is installed on. Other times, malware bundled with regular-looking apps and games can allow hackers to steal usernames, passwords and session tokens from infected computers, which may let them log in as if they were a legitimate employee.

Binance will face questions about why the company’s security allowed a single employee’s laptop to access systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in funds.

Spokespeople for Binance did not respond to an email with questions about the breach. TechCrunch has also asked the company who, if anyone, performed a security audit of Binance’s network and systems prior to the hack. Companies regularly ask third-party companies to stress-test their security to identify weaknesses that could be exploited by attackers, but it’s unclear if Binance sought such a review.

Security researchers at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and forensic company, attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, and called it the “largest hack in history.” 

Researchers describe the network of hackers, known in the cybersecurity industry as TraderTraitor, as a North Korean cell focused almost exclusively on stealing crypto from large companies and exchanges. This group was also blamed for the now-second-largest heist on record, a $1.4 billion theft from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.

According to TRM, the theft of Binance’s billions in crypto took about 20 minutes.

Blockchain security firm Elliptic also attributed the Binance theft to North Korean hackers. Elliptic said some of the stolen funds ended up in the same wallet that was used in a previous cyberattack on crypto exchange Bitget earlier this year, in which hackers stole $351 million.

The U.S. government and its allies have long warned about the threat from North Korea, which remains cut off from the U.S. and the global financial system for its ongoing development of its nuclear weapons program. Researchers say the breakaway country’s sole motivations are to steal as much crypto as possible in order to continue developing its sanctioned weapons of mass destruction.

Updated with statement from Binance.

title: Apple fined $15.5 million as South Korea orders changes to App Store rules
snippet: Apple and Google were fined today in South Korea over their app payment practices, with regulators also ordering both companies to change several policies. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple and Google were fined today in South Korea over their app payment practices, with regulators also ordering both companies to change several policies. Here are the details.

Apple’s App Store woes keep mounting

South Korea’s Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) announced today a series of fines and corrective orders against Apple and Google over violations of the country’s Telecommunications Business Act.

Specifically for Apple, the KMCC imposed a fine of 20.81 billion won (approximately $15.5 million) and ordered the company to revise its App Store policies regarding payment methods and app review procedures, as well as prevent what it referred to as “discriminatory commission” practices from recurring.

In its announcement, the KMCC noted:

This is the first enforcement case under the 2021 amendment to the Telecommunications Business Act, which introduced prohibited acts for app market operators, such as forcing specific payment methods and unfairly delaying app reviews.

In essence, the decision centers around three violations: forcing specific payment methods, unfairly delaying app reviews, and imposing discriminatory commissions.

On the payment methods front, the KMCC said Apple and Google “effectively forced” developers to use their own in-app payment systems by imposing a 26% commission and additional restrictions on third-party alternatives.

“This constitutes an act in which an app market operator unfairly uses its position in transactions to force mobile content providers and others to use a specific payment method,” the KMCC said.

As a result, Apple and Google must revise their policies to allow external payment methods and address restrictions imposed on developers using alternative payment systems.

As for the app review process, the KMCC found that Apple and Google “delayed app reviews, for example by not providing specific reasons when reviews were delayed or not clearly responding to individual inquiries about the reasons for delays and expected timelines.”

Accordingly, Apple and Google must revise their app review procedures to address these issues.

Finally, on the discriminatory commissions, which applied only to Apple, the KMCC found that between July 2015 and January 2023, the company calculated its 30% commission differently for South Korean and overseas developers. While overseas developers were charged based on prices excluding value-added tax (VAT), South Korean developers were charged based on prices including VAT.

“KMCC determined that this constituted an act of unfairly providing rates, numbers, telecommunications facilities, or other economic benefits for telecommunications services or bundled services in a discriminatory manner compared to other users […].”

The KMCC said Apple will also have to take measures to prevent discriminatory commission practices between South Korean and overseas developers from recurring.

According to Reuters, Apple said it “‌disagreed ⁠with the decision and was evaluating options in accordance with South Korean ​laws.” ​Apple added that “⁠it has worked with outside developers ​to enable innovation ​through ⁠its App Store.”

Today’s decision comes on the heels of similar regulatory pressure in other markets, including Brazil and Japan, where Apple has introduced alternative app distribution and payment options in response to local competition rules.

The company has also faced years of scrutiny in the European Union, where it recently overhauled its App Store fees and business terms to address concerns raised by the European Commission.

fullText:
Binance has disclosed that $6.3 billion worth of crypto funds have been stolen from the platform, in what’s believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency hack on record. In a series of updates posted to X, the crypto exchange said that user funds are safe, and that around $3 billion of the impacted assets have been frozen so far.

Binance has publicly committed to covering any losses resulting from the hack. The company has an emergency reserve fund of around $1.3 billion (at last valuation) to protect user assets in these situations, and said it has also reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident — $5 billion of which is “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.”

“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” Binance reported on X. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”

The company shared details about the compromised laptop that belongs to one of its DevOps engineers in a prior update, saying it allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Deposits and withdrawals have been suspended in response to the hack, and the affected address has had its authorization revoked.

“To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions, and this was not a single ‘one-click’ action. It involved a more complex attack process,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. “Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”

Binance may not be pointing fingers at who’s behind the attack, but blockchain analysis firms TRM and Chainalysis both attribute it to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime hacking group that has a history of stealing funds from cryptocurrency exchanges. This is the largest known cryptocurrency heist in history — four times higher than the previous record, when $1.46 billion was stolen from Bybit last year — and according to TRM, most of the theft occurred over a period of just 20 minutes.

This isn’t the first time Binance has been hacked, having suffered a previous security breach in 2019 in which $40 million worth of crypto assets (valued at the time) were stolen. The latest hack comes as cases of large-scale crypto theft are escalating, however, after several heists were disclosed by crypto companies in September. There are also new concerns around how AI tools can be used maliciously against the industry, with OpenAI reporting earlier this month that one of its models managed to swipe fake crypto on an Ethereum test network it didn’t have access to.

“This is an extraordinary hack, for its size and for the response... Few financial systems have ever shown a theft of this scale,” TRM chief policy officer Ari Redbord said in a statement to Sky News. “The theft shows how exposed the system is to sophisticated attackers moving at a speed we have never seen.”

title: iOS 27.2 introduces new age verification feature using selfie
snippet: iOS 27.2 is here, and it introduces a new feature for age verification using a selfie. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 is here, and it introduces a new feature for age verification using a selfie. Here are the details.

Apple offers new, privacy-focused way to verify your age in iOS 27.2

An increasing number of territories around the world now require iPhone age verification in certain scenarios, such as when creating an Apple Account, updating your software, downloading apps, or changing select settings.

Per Apple, these requirements may apply to users in Australia, Brazil, Singapore, South Korea, the UK, and also the United States (Texas).

While iOS already offered other methods of age verification, such as using a credit card or scanning your ID, iOS 27.2 adds a new option: taking a selfie.

Per a new support document, Apple says:

In some states, countries, or regions, you might be asked to confirm that you’re an adult before you can take certain actions on your Apple Account. One way to confirm that you’re an adult is to take a selfie. An age-estimation model will then evaluate the images of your face.

The selfie option isn’t available in all regions, but if you’re asked to confirm you’re an adult, you might see the option to use a selfie. 

Here’s how it works per Apple’s instructions:

Choose the option to take a selfie, then tap Get Started.

Hold your device in front of you and center your face in the frame.

Capture all four angles of your face by moving your head slowly right, left, up, and down. Follow the onscreen guidance to complete confirmation. It might take a moment to estimate your age.

Apple says your privacy is protected by its age-estimation models running both on-device and on Private Cloud Compute. The selfie “isn’t accessible to anyone, not even Apple.” And after your age has been confirmed, the selfie is deleted immediately and “isn’t retained in any form.”

To learn more about Apple’s new age verification feature in iOS 27.2, read the full support document here.

fullText:
Good morning! Today I’m reading about the death of the internet, deciding whether to buy a PROLED or many pro LEDs, building all my IKEA furniture with this step-by-step 3D app, trying desperately to get into the Readwise Books early access, and playing an “Enhanced 3D” Command & Conquer: Red Alert on my PC.

Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Alphabet’s Q3 earnings were interesting. Despite a 25% rise in revenue and a healthy net income of $26 billion, analysts were disappointed with the company’s results, sending the stock down as much as 11% in after-hours trading.

	

On the plus side, the company’s cloud business is booming, doubling year-over-year revenue to $30 billion as it attracts frontier labs to its data centers. But advertising revenue didn’t meet expectations, and investors appear to be worried that its search advertising business, one of the most efficient sources of recurring revenue in history, is not keeping up with changing user behavior.

As Anthropic gets ready to soar into its IPO later this year, mature businesses like Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon are racing to adapt to a market where demand for AI infrastructure is outpacing compute supply. But investors are looking at the capital expenditure tied up in future data center buildouts and getting nervous that, if the bubble bursts, even these well-capitalized companies will take massive hits.

The biggest question surrounding Google’s stock performance is whether it can sufficiently monetize AI-powered search before demand for its traditional search inventory falls off a cliff. As the company sends less and less traffic to the open web, it’s touting the fact that AI Mode and AI Overviews keep people on Google for three times as long as traditional search.

So it’s no surprise that it’s expanding ads in AI Mode to 10 new markets this week, with more to come by the end of the year. While the post was only a few paragraphs long, expanding its AI ad business may end up being one of the company’s most consequential announcements of 2026.

✉️ Inbox

OnePlus rolling out ColorOS to OnePlus 13, others as Android 17 update expands. Mixed feelings about this one, but glad to see OPPO is honoring its promise to OnePlus owners.

Android Find Hub app reveals how ‘Left Behind’ and ‘Ring your phone’ alerts work on Pixel Tag. Hard to believe the Pixel Tag still isn’t available given it was announced in August.

Vivo’s X500 series launches globally with MediaTek chips and insane cameras. Like the OPPO Find X10 Max, Vivo’s new flagship is ridiculous in all the best ways.

Someone is bringing Android Auto back to your phone’s screen, and it actually works. This little sideloaded hack fakes Android Auto on your smartphone for those who don’t want to deal with Google’s current disaster of a solution.

Gemini Notebook for Android, iOS adds built-in audio recorder. The best tool for cheating on optimizing your homework just got even better.

Samsung’s open-ear Galaxy Buds On cost $229 in the US, launching next month. They’re no Beans, and they’re also very expensive. Good luck with these, Samsung.

Samsung can’t decide between a larger Galaxy Z Fold 9 or one with worse specs, and neither can I. Here’s my hot take: we need fewer, not more, foldable options. Keep the lineup focused.

Motorola’s flagship Signature 27 sounds quite expensive in retail leak. Motorola is cooking lately, but this phone looks a little too rich for my blood.

Public Discord messages might start showing up in Google Search, unless users opt out

RAMageddon is ready to rage on through 2030. We get the world we deserve, and that means more expensive gadgets on which to use many, many AI tokens.

Amazon’s latest Echo smart displays and speakers reinforce Google Home’s lost lead. I’m no fan of Alexa, but I have to admit Amazon is crushing it on the hardware design front lately.

Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform. Android’s Dev Summit yielded some really interesting announcements, and this was top among them.

Google Chrome rolling out ‘Suggested by Gemini’ autofill.

Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon with ‘significant gains across coding and agentic tasks’. Two weeks after Argon comes Carbon. What happened to Barium? Guess it was stuck in the loo.

Some Pixel Watch users report a sudden decrease in battery life

➡️ FWD:

I didn’t get to see either of the first Dune movies on IMAX, but you can bet your ass I’ve already secured opening-day tickets for the third one. Dune: Part Three debuts in December, and we now have the final trailer that showcases the impending showdown between Muad’Dib and Chani as the former realizes the consequences of his galactic war.

On the gadgety side, there’s another impending showdown brewing between XREAL’s Android XR-powered Aura glasses and Meta’s upcoming VR Glasses. 

I liked Jasmine Uniza’s video below comparing the two because, until I watched it, I didn’t realize the extent of the diverging approaches to reality they’re each taking. The Aura glasses are more traditionally translucent and somewhat awkwardly project two OLED screens on top of the dimmed lenses, allowing the outside world to filter through. Meta’s VR Glasses eschew the traditional headset shape and weight of the Quest but block out far more of the outside world and use external cameras, like their predecessors, to pipe in mixed-reality footage.

Finally, some personal news of a sort: I am now a permanent host of The Sideload. If you know me at all, you know I love a podcast, and Will Sattelberg was my co-host at the Android Police podcast for three years before he left for 9to5 last year. I’m so excited to be doing this again every week with him, and I hope you’ll tune in to our most recent episode about the death of the web browser and other good news.

🗑️ Trash

If you’ve been patiently waiting for Apple’s top-tier M5 Ultra-powered Mac Studio, fear not: Apple has you covered. From 9to5Mac:

When Apple announced the new M5 Max and M5 Ultra configurations of the Mac Studio in August, it said a configuration with 512GB of RAM would be available in October. Today, the company officially revealed the pricing of that option.

If you head to the Mac Studio configurator on Apple’s website, you’ll see the new 512GB upgrade option. As previously announced, the 512GB option is only available with the top-tier M5 Ultra chip that has a 36-core CPU and 80‑core GPU.

It’s a $15,500 upgrade over the base configuration of that processor, which has 96GB of unified memory.

To put it another way: you’ll pay $22,299 for the Mac Studio with the top-tier M5 Ultra, 512GB of unified memory, and 1TB of storage. You can spec it up all the way to 16TB of storage, which brings the total price to $29,799.00.

title: The HomeView and Echo Show 16 could be the family computers I’ve been asking for
snippet: Three years ago, I wrote an obituary for the smart display. The category - smart speakers with touchscreens attached - was stuck with a few underpowered gadgets from Google and Amazon that tried to do too much and did too little well. Back then, I also laid out what they needed to do to improve. This month, Apple and Amazon launched new smart displays that check nearly every box on that list. Based on my brief hands-on time with Apple's first smart display, the $299 HomeView, and Amazon's $499.99 Echo Show 16, a ground-up rebuild of its smart display line, these could finally turn the smart display into what it should have been all along: … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Three years ago, I wrote an obituary for the smart display. The category — smart speakers with touchscreens attached — was stuck with a few underpowered gadgets from Google and Amazon that tried to do too much and did too little well. Back then, I also laid out what they needed to do to improve. This month, Apple and Amazon launched new smart displays that check nearly every box on that list.

Based on my brief hands-on time with Apple’s first smart display, the $299 HomeView, and Amazon’s $499.99 Echo Show 16, a ground-up rebuild of its smart display line, these could finally turn the smart display into what it should have been all along: the family computer. Not a place to do homework or pay the bills, but a shared screen the whole household can use to check the calendar, see who’s at the door, and figure out what’s for dinner.

Apple’s HomeView has a clean, simple interface.

The biggest shift is that both companies have finally brought computer-class hardware to the space: Apple with its A18 chip (the same as in the MacBook Neo) and Liquid Retina display, and Amazon with a MediaTek processor and the same Nanomatte display as its new Alexa Tablet. This turns a category plagued by underpowered hardware and limited software into devices people might actually want to use.

The catch is price. In 2023, the Echo Show 5 cost $85 and the Nest Hub $99. Apple’s HomeView, the cheaper of the two new models, costs three times that. But these devices now have a much clearer purpose, beyond being a vessel for each company’s revamped voice assistant. And with the software to back it up, they might actually be worth the investment.

The Echo Show 16 offers a more tablet-style interface, with options for a calendar or a smart home dashboard.

As our lives have become increasingly digital, the need for a central place to corral all the information required to run a busy household has only grown. For years, the calendar, grocery list, meal plan, and chores all lived inside one person’s phone, creating an exhausting mental load. Add in the connected home, and the need for a communal device grows even greater: an interface anyone in the house can use to check who is at the door without opening it, adjust the thermostat, or dim all the lights with a tap or a quick voice command. Yes, some devices can do some of these things, but none do them all well.

The popularity of devices like the Skylight Calendar shows the need for a communal household screen. And while a tablet might seem like a natural fit, it has two challenges: limited multiuser support, and anything with a battery will wander into someone’s bedroom and die under a pillow. I learned that from personal experience. I thought Google’s Pixel Tablet, a hybrid tablet and smart display, was the category’s next evolution, though I wasn’t wild about its detachable screen. That turned out to be a big problem in my house — along with its half-baked smart home support. Google reportedly canceled its successor 18 months later.

HomeView has some built-in apps, and it relies on your iPhone to run others.

With their new devices, Apple and Amazon are bringing three things to the category that I’ve been wanting for years: computer-class hardware, a display built for sharing that can easily switch between users, and a screen that is always on and as easy to use as a light switch. No PIN to enter or screensaver to swipe away, just reach out and tap to control your lights or scroll through your calendar. Both the HomeView and Echo Show 16 appear to solve these problems. (Of course, I’ll need to test them properly to be sure.)

Apple’s approach treats the person as the user; HomeView is designed to know you

However, that’s where the similarities end. What I find fascinating about these two side-by-side product launches is the different approach each company is taking to fit these devices into your household.

Amazon has built one screen for the household that works without your phone — you don’t even need one to set it up (although it helps). Apple has built a screen that is an extension of your phone; it has communal features, but they’re limited compared with what you can do if you connect your phone.

The Echo Show 16 has a new meal planning feature as part of its Family Management homescreen.

The reason for the split is obvious: Apple is built around the iPhone; Amazon is built around, well, everything else. Apple’s approach treats the person as the user; HomeView is designed to know you. In Apple’s demo, Siri AI knew exactly when your friend would arrive at the front door from the airport based on reading your text messages and could turn on the coffee machine so their espresso was ready the moment they walked in. But while HomeView has communal features, most of the good stuff seems to appear only when HomeView recognizes your face and your phone is nearby.

Amazon’s approach treats the household as the user; the Echo Show is designed to know your home

Amazon’s approach treats the household as the user; the Echo Show is designed to know your home. The company’s Omnisense technology built into its devices can sense presence, temperature, and room acoustics throughout your home. One of Amazon’s demos showed that when someone walks up your driveway, a figure appears on a map of your home, and you can tap it to see a live view of their approach through your Ring camera. While Amazon doesn’t have the same personal context as an iPhone, the Echo Show 16 offers broader features for the household, including meal planning, a full Fire TV, and a color-coded household calendar.

Amazon is selling a maximal feature set at a premium price designed for everyone while Apple is pushing a more polished, narrower product at a lower price, aimed squarely at its existing users. I’m looking forward to seeing which approach works best once I have these devices in my home. But for the first time in years, I’m excited about testing a smart display. I guess my obituary was premature.

title: Binance pauses withdrawals as hackers suspected of stealing billions in crypto
snippet: Some estimates say hackers stole billions in crypto from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, during a cyberattack on Thursday.
fullText:
Binance has confirmed to TechCrunch that it is dealing with a security incident as users reported that funds were being drained from the crypto exchange’s wallets.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch that it is “aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.”

“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement.  

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”

Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary said that Binance has “temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks following a security incident as a precautionary measure.”

News of the breach comes hours after Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said in a post on X that the company likely had been hacked. Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered” but did not provide an explanation for the claim.

Financial tech giant Circle froze about $800 million in Tether as it passed through its networks, while crypto giant Tether froze about $1.56 billion related to Binance’s hack.

Crypto watchers say at least $2 billion has been drained from Binance’s hot wallets, which are internet-connected cryptocurrency wallets that store crypto that are connected to the internet. By some estimates, Binance may have lost upward of $5.7 billion in crypto, though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing.

It’s unclear who is behind the hack, and Binance did not say if it had received any correspondence from the hackers. 

If confirmed into the billions, this would likely rank as one of the largest crypto breaches in history, according to leaderboards tracking crypto thefts.

In 2025, hackers stole a record $1.4 billion in crypto in a single breach from exchange Bybit, blamed on North Korean hackers.

In what appears to be a separate incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market giant Polymarket briefly halted trading after it confirmed that a third-party company was compromised, which led to the company pausing withdrawals. According to security researchers, hackers stole around $2 million in user funds after compromising a piece of software developed by a company called DebugBear.

title: Reddit will soon be a ‘logged-in-only’ website, forcing you to have an account
snippet: Reddit is shifting to a “logged-in-only experience,” the company confirmed during its latest earnings call. more…
fullText:
Reddit is shifting to a “logged-in-only experience,” the company confirmed during its latest earnings call.

While the timeline is vague at this point, Reddit has confirmed that it will be locking down the site for users without an account, also impacting usage in private browsing modes. CEO Steve Huffman explains in a shareholder letter and a post on Reddit that the website will becoming a “logged-in-only experience.”

Moving to primarily logged-in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible, and can find the content and communities most relevant to them. It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally. It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world.

In Q4 we’ll begin fully testing this in select markets outside the U.S. The results of those tests will inform an optimized version of logged-in-only Reddit globally.

The change also comes as Reddit says that search referral traffic was “down meaningfully” in Q3 2026, mainly in regards to logged-out traffic. “Down meaningfully” was later detailed to mean that traffic “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week.”

As for private browsing, Huffman says that Reddit has “rebuilt and [is] re-releasing incognito mode in our app.” 

	

Details on what will and will not be available to logged-out users are unclear at this time, though Huffman says that “the front page being available logged-out is useful and important,” adding that “visitors arriving from search or other external sources to see the content that’s being linked to.” He further implies that AI scraping is certainly a major part of this decision, saying that “the vast majority of unauthorized access to Reddit (basically the scraping and stealing of Reddit’s data) happens through our logged-out experiences.”

This comes shortly after Reddit rolled out a new personalized “For You” homepage.

title: New M6 Macs buck Apple’s second wave of price hikes
snippet: In addition to the spec bumps, today’s M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro announcements came with an extra piece of good news: prices remained unchanged from the previous generations, unlike several other recent Apple product launches that brought another round of increases. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In addition to the spec bumps, today’s M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro announcements came with an extra piece of good news: prices remained unchanged from the previous generations, unlike several other recent Apple product launches that brought another round of increases. Here are the details.

Prices unchanged, for a change

Earlier today, Apple announced two new M6-powered Macs, which start at the same prices as their predecessors.

And while both models benefit from the faster M6 chip, iMac buyers are also getting more CPU and GPU cores for the same price, as the base model now comes with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, up from the 8-core CPU and 8-core GPU in the previous generation’s M4 chip.

As 9to5Mac readers probably remember, Apple raised prices across much of its product lineup in June, including the iMac, which went from $1,299 to $1,499, and the 14-inch MacBook Pro, which went from $1,699 to $1,999.

At the time, the company also hiked prices for the HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, and iPad mini, all of which saw new versions announced recently with yet another price bump.

The HomePod mini, which went from $99 to $129 in June, now costs $149 with the second-generation model. The Apple TV 4K, which previously started at $129, jumped to $199 in June, while the new generation starts at $299 (albeit with twice the storage). And the iPad mini, which went from $499 to $599 in June, now starts at $699 with the OLED model announced earlier this week.

And while iPhone prices were left untouched during the June increases, that changed in September with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which now start at $1,199 and $1,299, respectively, up $100 from their predecessors.

Apple also raised prices by $100 for the older iPhone models still in its lineup, including the iPhone 17, iPhone Air, and iPhone 17e.

	

With that in mind, although the new M6-powered Macs are far from cheap, it’s still good news that they didn’t come with another price hike on top of the June increases.

Things are looking way less promising for those waiting for tomorrow’s expected OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models, however, with Bloomberg reporting that Apple has discussed a $2,899 starting price for the 14-inch model. If Apple applies the same rumored $400 premium to the current 16-inch model, which starts at $2,999, the new version could cost $3,399 or more.

That, in turn, makes Apple’s decision to keep prices unchanged for today’s M6-powered Macs all the more welcome, especially for buyers who were already dreading the possibility of having to shell out even more after waiting for the new models. Whether that will hold remains to be seen.

What’s your take on Apple’s pricing strategy for the M6 Macs announced earlier today? Let us know in the comments.

title: Last-minute leak reveals new touchscreen MacBook Pro details: pricing, new cooling system, more
snippet: In a roundup of what to expect from tomorrow’s “Pro and Tell” event, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman shared new details about the upcoming OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models. Here’s what to expect. more…
fullText:
In a roundup of what to expect from tomorrow’s “Pro and Tell” event, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman shared new details about the upcoming OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models. Here’s what to expect.

Report reveals last-minute details and backstory of rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro

Tomorrow, Apple is expected to announce its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro models, featuring OLED displays, Dynamic Island, and a thinner, lighter design.

While previous reports have suggested that the new models will come with significantly higher prices, Bloomberg now offers more specific figures, along with additional details about their redesign.

According to Gurman’s sources, “Apple has discussed charging $2,899 for the new 14-inch model with an M5 Pro chip,” which, if Apple applies at least the same $400 premium to the 16-inch model, would mean “the new version will cost at least $3,399.”

Compared to the $2,199 and $2,699 starting prices of the 14-inch and 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro models before Apple’s June price hikes, that would represent an increase of at least $700 in just four months.

Gurman added that “Apple plans to continue selling the non-touch versions alongside the new machines,” and further commented on that in a post on X:

I do not expect the current non-touch MacBook Pros (14 inch at $2499 and 16-inch at $2999) to go anywhere tomorrow. Retail stores are fully stocked up on those as well still. https://t.co/UTs2NJ1N3A

— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 27, 2026

In other words, he expects the new OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro models to sit at the top of Apple’s current laptop lineup, rather than replacing the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max models.

However, users looking to get the redesigned hardware will likely have to pay the premium, regardless of whether they actually want a touchscreen.

At $2,899, the 14-inch model would mark the highest starting price for a new MacBook Pro model, surpassing the $2,799 Apple charged for a 17-inch version introduced in 2006. The pricing would also put Apple among the most expensive makers of touch-screen laptops, alongside premium offerings from Dell Technologies Inc. that also feature OLED displays.

Beyond the OLED touchscreen, Gurman reaffirmed that the new MacBook Pro models will feature a slightly thinner design, thinner bezels, a noticeably lighter body, and a redesigned hinge to prevent the screen from moving when touched, all of which we covered earlier today here.

The report also adds a new detail: Apple has reworked the cooling system to improve airflow through the hinge while helping reduce the computers’ weight.

	

Finally, Gurman’s report offers some behind-the-scenes details about how Apple decided to bring touchscreens to the Mac. According to his sources, Tim Cook greenlit the touchscreen MacBook Pro project roughly four years ago, in part because the feature had become one of the most requested by Apple customers.

“He said we should just do it,” according to a person with knowledge of the decision.

Gurman added that Ternus oversaw development of the new MacBook Pro models. According to the report, Ternus believed “Apple had fallen behind in the area and indicated internally that touch screens had become table stakes for laptops, making it time for the company to embrace the technology.”

According to the report, Apple plans to open preorders for the new touchscreen MacBook Pro models tomorrow, October 28, with availability potentially beginning as early as November 6, alongside the new M6-powered Macs announced today.

title: Apple releases iOS 27.2, here’s what’s new
snippet: Apple has officially released iOS 27.2 for iPhone. The update brings a new look to Apple Music, more Siri AI languages, changes to Messages and Podcasts, and Apple Pencil support for iPhone Duo. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple has officially released iOS 27.2 for iPhone. The update brings a new look to Apple Music, more Siri AI languages, changes to Messages and Podcasts, and Apple Pencil support for iPhone Duo. Here’s what’s new.

Release notes

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week

Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List

Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting

Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need

Siri AI is available in more languages, with support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Siri AI is not available in the EU or mainland China

Other

Suggestions in Messages help you take action based on the context of your conversations, like adding a Calendar invite for a dinner

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

The Home tab in the Podcasts app offers two separate sections for New Episodes and Continue Playing, letting you find the latest updates from your shows and then pick up where you left off

Friends tab in the Games app provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages

Simple Profiles in the Apple TV app lets everyone in your household have their own profile, with recommendations that fit what they like to watch

FaceTime supports adding a third party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call

Here’s what we’ve seen from testing as well.

Apple Pencil support for iPhone Duo

iPhone Duo gains support for Apple Pencil with iOS 27.2. Apple originally announced the feature as coming later this year, and it’s arriving with this update.

There is one detail to keep in mind: iPhone Duo works with Apple Pencil (USB-C). Apple Pencil Pro and other Pencil models aren’t supported. More on Apple Pencil support.

Apple Music gets a new look

Apple Music has a new black-and-white app icon that replaces the familiar red design. Inside the app, blue replaces red as the accent color for the selected tab. Apple has also refreshed Music widgets with black backgrounds. More on the Apple Music changes.

Messages, Podcasts, and Apple TV updates

Messages gains Suggested Actions, which offer shortcuts based on the conversation. A message about plans, for example, can include an option to create a calendar event or reminder. Settings also lets you control which types of suggestions appear.

Apple Podcasts separates new episodes from episodes you’ve already started. New Episodes and Continue Playing give each category its own place on the Home tab.

The Apple TV app also adds profiles on iPhone, letting users keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. More on the app updates.

More Siri AI languages and Group FaceTime Dual Capture

Siri AI adds support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

Meanwhile, Dual Capture expands to Group FaceTime. The feature lets you share views from the front and rear cameras simultaneously. More on these additions.

New Home controls

The Home app adds Lock After Closing and Door Left Open options for compatible smart locks. These let you automatically lock a door after it closes or receive an alert if it stays open too long. More on the smart lock features.

HomePod owners also gain a Lock Controls setting after updating both their iPhone and HomePod to 27.2. This prevents unwanted taps from starting audio, while preserving touch responses for features like timers and alarms. More on HomePod Lock Controls.

What about the new Health app?

Apple’s redesigned Health app appeared in earlier iOS 27.2 betas, but Apple removed it before release. The upgrade is still planned for later this year. More on the Health app release timing.

You can install iOS 27.2 by opening Settings > General > Software Update on your iPhone.

title: Apple addressed at least 329 unique security vulnerabilities across today’s system updates
snippet: Apple has updated its security releases page with details of the vulnerabilities addressed in today’s updates to iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and Safari. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has updated its security releases page with details of the vulnerabilities addressed in today’s updates to iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and Safari. Here are the details.

Apple details security releases from today’s updates

Whenever Apple releases software updates, the company also usually updates its security releases page with details of the vulnerabilities addressed.

Today, the company updated the page with the security content for the following system updates:

Name and information link

Available for

iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2

iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 4th generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 2nd generation and later, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later

iOS 26.7.2 and iPadOS 26.7.2

iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 3rd generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 1st generation and later, iPad Air 3rd generation and later, iPad 8th generation and later, and iPad mini 5th generation and later

iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11

iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, iPad 7th generation

macOS Golden Gate 27.2

macOS Golden Gate

macOS Tahoe 26.7.2

macOS Tahoe

macOS Sequoia 15.8.2

macOS Sequoia

tvOS 27.2

Apple TV 4K 2nd generation and later

watchOS 27.2

Apple Watch Series 9 and later

visionOS 27.2

Apple Vision Pro (all models)

Safari 27.2

macOS Sequoia and macOS Tahoe

tvOS 26.6.1

This update has no published CVE entries.

Apple TV HD and Apple TV 4K 1st generation

In total, Apple addressed 329 unique security vulnerabilities across today’s software releases. Many of these vulnerabilities affect multiple operating systems, resulting in a whopping combined total of 1,265 CVE listings.

These numbers may still increase, as Apple regularly adds new entries and updates existing ones in its security advisories after their initial publication.

Among the most notable security fixes are a CoreMedia issue that could let a malicious app access the camera on an iPhone, iPad, Mac, or Apple Vision Pro without permission (CVE-2026-86990), and an Apple Intelligence vulnerability that could let a remote attacker access sensitive user data on supported iPhones and iPads (CVE-2026-86987).

Apple also addressed a Siri vulnerability in macOS Tahoe that could let an app access sensitive user data (CVE-2026-43736), along with multiple WebKit flaws that could allow maliciously crafted web content to execute arbitrary code.

Specifically, when it comes to WebKit, Apple has been on a security-patching spree in recent months, partly driven by the growing use of AI tools to uncover vulnerabilities. (In today’s updates alone, Apple credited AI tools and research teams for several vulnerabilities across its software.)

Earlier this year, the company also released multiple updates to fix flaws exploited by Coruna and DarkSword on older devices. Both exploit kits used WebKit vulnerabilities as part of attack chains that compromised iPhones running older versions of iOS.

And speaking of older versions of iOS, today’s updates also bring a previously released CoreGraphics fix to devices still running iOS 18 and iPadOS 18. The vulnerability could allow a maliciously crafted file to trigger arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-86950).

Apple first addressed the issue in updates released last month, warning that it may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals running versions of iOS before iOS 27.

You can check out the security fixes included in each update through the links above. For Apple’s complete security releases page, follow ⁠this link.

title: Waymo taps Toyota to supply robotaxis for Japan and the U.K.
snippet: Waymo will begin testing self-driving versions of Toyota's electric bZ4X vehicles in Japan next year as part of a broader partnership with the automaker.
fullText:
Image Credits:Waymo /	

	

						

12:01 AM PDT · October 30, 2026

											

			

Waymo will begin testing autonomous Toyota bZ4X vehicles in Japan next year as part of a broader partnership with the automaker to provide electric vehicles for robotaxi operations in international markets, including the U.K.

Under the partnership announced Friday, Toyota will manufacture the 2027 bZ4X vehicles and integrate Waymo’s self-driving system at its Takaoka factory in Japan. (The electric vehicle is now known as the BZ in the North American market)

The autonomous bZ4X vehicles will initially be tested in Japan, where Waymo intends to eventually operate a robotaxi service. But the intent is to deploy these vehicles in other right-hand driving countries such as the U.K.  Waymo has been testing its autonomous Jaguar I-Pace vehicles in London for months and plans to launch a robotaxi service there once it receives the necessary permits. 

The announcement comes 18 months after Toyota and Waymo signed a preliminary agreement to explore the development and deployment of an autonomous vehicle platform. At the time, the agreement fell into the “let’s see what happens” category, with language vague enough to leave plenty of room for interpretation. 

For now,  the partnership looks more like a conventional vehicle supplier deal that helps Waymo fill specific regional needs while adding a new model to its robotaxi portfolio.  

But the partnership could go beyond robotaxis. The companies said they will continue to look at bringing Waymo’s autonomous technology to personally owned Toyota vehicles. 

Toyota and Waymo also announced plans to look at other future “initiatives” that would use “insights from Waymo’s real-world operations” to improve safety for other road users. What that might mean is unclear, although Hiroki Nakajima, executive vice president of Toyota and a board member, provided some clues. 

“This collaboration will help scale that technology and bring it to customers in Japan and beyond through Waymo’s ride-hailing service, and in parallel, Toyota will continue to explore how integrating vehicles with traffic infrastructure can make those roads safer still,” he said in a statement.

title: You Can Spend Nearly $15K on Apple’s New Touchscreen MacBook Pro. Why?
snippet: Maxing out the new touchscreen MacBook Pro with a M5 Max chip and 16TB of storage will cost more than buying 10 basic MacBook Air laptops.
fullText:
The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, announced on Wednesday and available on Nov. 6, brings touchscreen control to Apple’s most premium laptop. Pricing starts at $2,899 for the entry-level M5 Pro with the smaller 14-inch display, or $3,399 for the 16-inch model, before any applicable education discounts.

If you go ham on Apple’s preorder configurator and max out the processor, memory and storage, the price balloons to an eye-watering $14,549. That’s wild, especially in today’s economy. Will anyone actually spend that?

Fully loading the M5 MacBook Pro

Let’s see what it means to reach that top-tier configuration of the new touchscreen laptop, starting with the larger, more expensive 16-inch PROLED XDR model at $3,399. Color doesn’t affect price, so take your pick of silver or space black.

			

More from CNET

The first upgrade you’ll pay for is Nano-texture glass, an antireflective glass finish physically etched at the nanometer scale to diffuse ambient light and eliminate glare, for an additional $150. 

Then, stepping up from the M5 Pro’s 20-core GPU to the M5 Max’s 35-core GPU brings the total to $4,949. Bumping to the even more potent 40-core GPU adds another $300, while unlocking horsepower for complex tasks like gaming, video editing and AI-driven operations such as machine learning and coding. (In our testing, CNET found that the Max 40-core is the best fit for pro creatives who work with 8K or raw video, data scientists and intensive users of generative AI imaging and video.) 

Next comes memory and storage, which is where things get really expensive. Our starting M5 Max configuration comes standard with 48GB of unified memory and 2TB of storage, but we can pump those numbers considerably. Upgrading to 128GB of memory adds $2,000. Going for 16TB of storage adds $7,000, the most expensive upgrade on the list, roughly doubling the price of the machine. 

Pricey high-capacity memory and storage were par for the course long before the RAMpocalypse, but the current AI-fueled spike in RAM and solid-state storage prices has made things worse.

“It’s so expensive because 16TB drives cost a fortune, as does 128GB, and professionals have been paying those workstation prices for years,” Lori Grunin, CNET senior editor for computers and gaming hardware, told me.

Maxing the RAM boosts bandwidth and performance, allowing the Mac to more easily work with the massive files used in high-resolution video, complex 3D models, large datasets and complex mathematical equations. The extra terabytes of storage mean more and larger files can be saved to the device, since neither the MacBook’s memory nor storage can be upgraded after purchase. 

All in, our fully loaded MacBook Pro M5 Max with 16-inch PROLED XDR Display comes to $14,549. 

Grunin said she’d want more for the money. “For that price, I’d expect the M5 Ultra chip,” she said. “But I don’t think they can put the Ultra in a laptop yet.”

The top-spec MacBooks are aimed at companies that can absorb the high costs of high-capacity storage and memory.Apple

These upgrades aren’t for everyday people

So who buys a laptop that costs more than a used car? Is this just a flex for the super-rich?

“It’s for people who don’t have to pay for it,” said CNET Managing Editor Joshua Goldman.

Configured-to-order, powerful mobile workstations like these are most commonly bought through enterprise procurement by companies, startups and institutions — so the employer is paying, not the individual. Think engineering and architecture firms, Hollywood VFX and post-production houses or AI, machine learning and data science teams. They have big budgets, can put the extra digital horsepower to use and can easily absorb the exorbitant price.

For context, Grunin pointed me to a Dell Precision workstation that I was able to trick out to over $18,000. Five-figure enterprise-scale machines from HP or Lenovo are also not out of the question.

Yes, there will be well-heeled individuals buying at this level, but they’re a relatively small slice of the pie. More likely, the majority of the new touch-enabled MacBook Pros sold will be at still-expensive but easier-to-fathom prices.
