title: The MacBook Pro OLED Isn’t the Touchscreen Mac I Was Looking For
snippet: Commentary: Apple finally put touch on a MacBook Pro, but at a price and form that confuses me.
fullText:
I’ve been on a mission for a decade and a half to see that Apple fuses its iPad and Mac lines into something that would be the best of both worlds. I’ve been told that iPads and Macs would never merge, and that touch would never come to Macs. Well, Macs have touchscreens now, or at least one of them; the awkwardly named “MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display” is the very first, arriving Nov. 6.

I’ve been reviewing iPads for years, and I also specialize in reviewing new forms of computing, such as VR/AR headsets and AI-enabled wearables. My hope is that these devices would evolve into true computers that could replace my laptop.

iPads have come awfully close, but the OS and app compatibility still creates a slight divide, meaning certain pro apps and browser tools don’t work the same way. But iPads have the form, the touchscreens, the transforming designs, the modular accessories and support for the wonderful Pencil. I argued earlier this year that the MacBook Neo, with a similar-to-iPad price and an iPhone/iPad-level chipset, showed how close Macs and iPads are getting. I can see a connecting thread, and it excites me.

			

More from CNET

I say all this because the new MacBook Pros, which I haven’t tried myself, add touchscreens but barely do anything at all to the laptop’s design itself. Instead of folding back or even flat, the screen hinge merely tilts to standard laptop angles and hangs in place while you touch the upright surface. 

While Apple is pitching the new MacBook touch features as a great way to interact with MacOS, it doesn’t look, at first glance, that MacOS has evolved to accommodate touch input in truly transformative ways…or in workflows that already perform wonderfully on iPhones and iPads.

Clearly, to me at least, Apple is on a transformation path. The iPhone Duo fuses parts of iPhone and iPad and aims to augment the phone experience with that of a tablet. Similar opportunities lie ahead for Macs and iPads: sure, you may not want MacOS as it exists now on an iPad, but I’d definitely want a touch-evolved MacOS fusion to live on an iPad that could transform into every Mac/iPad need I desire. Would that be worth a higher price? Sure.

The touchscreen MacBook Pro we’re getting at the end of 2026 isn’t that computer. It’s not something most people can afford, anyway, at $2,899 and up. But when I think of touch on a Mac, kids and families using it come to mind. Or, drawing with the Apple Pencil, which you can’t do on this touchscreen MacBook. Or having it be a useful way to access apps that currently live on iPads and iPhones and could, in a pinch, run on the Mac. For iMacs, it could be fun. For convertible MacBooks, it could redefine what a Mac is relative to an iPad.

All I can think of is, what if this Mac could fold back and work with Apple Pencil?Tara Brown/CNET

This feels like a foot in the door for Apple, and an odd one at that. The name “MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display” doesn’t even reference touch at all, and Apple’s marketing seems to underplay the touch-on-Mac debut. The real star of the show is the new OLED display, which truly is a pro feature for a MacBook. The touch extras feel like they’re added in as a bonus.

Now, it all could end up feeling better and more useful than I’m thinking right now. And yes, I’ve often reached up to my MacBook Air to touch the screen, especially after working on an iPad for a while. Almost all the other computers in 2026 have touchscreens, anyway, even in laptop form.

But with all the promises iPads already deliver on for touch, Macs deserve better. And I’m hoping 2027 is when Apple really gets into a transformative discussion about how touch-enabled Macs, and all existing and future iPads, can evolve next. The future Apple computer I’m envisioning doesn’t exist yet, but it’s getting close. And I’m optimistically thinking Apple can address it soon, but as always, you never know.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein

title: Apple knows the iPad mini market, but internet unimpressed by 60Hz
snippet: Apple yesterday officially launched what it describes as “the biggest update ever” to the iPad mini, featuring an OLED screen and a thinner, lighter design. However, while there are a significant number of upgrades, internet commentators were very focused on the one thing Apple didn’t upgrade: that 60Hz display … more…
fullText:
Apple yesterday officially launched what it describes as “the biggest update ever” to the iPad mini, featuring an OLED screen and a thinner, lighter design.

However, while there are a significant number of upgrades, internet commentators were very focused on the one thing Apple didn’t upgrade: that 60Hz display … 

Apple highlighted the new features.

A stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance with A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance. The larger 8.5-inch OLED display, also available with a nano-texture option, delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini for a brilliant and immersive viewing experience. A20 Pro supercharges AI with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. iPad mini now has a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge that’s perfect for video calls, an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support.

Commenters, however, were quick to point to the fact that the refresh rate wasn’t mentioned, with the obvious conclusion that it remains 60Hz instead of being updated to a ProMotion variable refresh rate of 1 to 120Hz.

“700 bucks and no 120hz display?”

“I was someone interested in adding a mini but at 60hz, 128gb, no Face ID I can’t justify the already inflated price tag.”

“60Hz right? in 2026 right? Hell no.”

“60Hz? Next…”

“60Hz in 2026. Apple should be ashamed.”

	

I could include many more quotes, but you get the idea. It’s certainly a surprising omission in a 2026 device, especially when our sister site 9to5Google noted that the closest Android competitor has a 185Hz refresh rate.

The biggest point in Redmagic’s favor is in that display, too. Where Apple is still refusing to give the iPad Mini a 120Hz refresh rate with this latest model – utterly insane in the year two thousand and twenty-six, if I do say so myself – Astra 2 has a 185Hz refresh rate. I’ve not found that inherently better than a standard 120Hz panel, but it’s way better than the 60Hz panel Apple’s latest will still be using.

Now I fully acknowledge that Apple knows the iPad mini market better than any of us do. I’m also aware that it has historically been primarily a business device, used for applications ranging from restaurant waitstaff relaying orders to the kitchen through mobile payment terminals to warehouse inventory systems. None of these types of applications would remotely benefit from a display with a faster refresh rate.

Additionally, when it comes to consumers, I’m sure it’s true that not everyone appreciates the benefits of 120Hz. Some of those in our comments claimed they couldn’t tell the difference, while others said it was only really relevant to gaming. Adding that category of individual purchasers to the majority business market, and Apple has undoubtedly correctly concluded that the majority of its customers simply don’t care about this feature. 

However … Those who do care about it, care about it rather a lot. I don’t know what the unit cost difference would be, but since 120Hz is now standard on a great many cheaper devices, I can’t imagine it’s a substantial one. I can’t help feeling that this is a case where Apple simply should have done the right thing, even if only a minority of buyers would appreciate it.

title: Amazon announced five new Alexa devices, including 16-inch Echo Show
snippet: Apple recently launched new HomePod mini speakers and its HomeView smart display, and today it’s Amazon’s turn with five new Alexa devices. This includes a new Echo speaker with visual intelligence and an Echo Show with a larger 16-inch display and a nanomatte option … more…
fullText:
Apple recently launched new HomePod mini speakers and its HomeView smart display, and today it’s Amazon’s turn with five new Alexa devices.

This includes a new Echo speaker with visual intelligence and an Echo Show with a larger 16-inch display and a nanomatte option …

Echo Dot

The latest smart device lineup kicks off with a next-generation Echo Dot speaker, which includes a home hub, on-device AI capabilities, and a built-in Wi-Fi extender.

For the first time, it includes a built-in smart home hub, so Alexa connects to thousands of compatible devices such as lights, locks, and thermostats right out of the box—plus a built-in eero Wi-Fi extender adds up to 1,000 square feet of coverage to your existing network. At its core is Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon, with a new AI Accelerator for on-device AI that sharpens conversational detection and filters out background noise. Music, audiobooks, and podcasts sound great on the new Echo Dot, with crisp vocals and 50% more bass than its predecessor.

The Dot is available today for $99.99, with special Kids editions for $109.99 that include a one-year subscription to Amazon Kids+.

Echo Studio with Home Camera

The Echo Studio is a better speaker that now includes HomePod-like room mapping and a camera that allows a live view of your home as well as Alexa-powered visual intelligence features.

Echo Studio with Home Camera takes Amazon’s best-sounding speaker and gives it a richer understanding of the room around it, making Alexa even more useful. The same powerful audio architecture is still at its core—a high-excursion woofer and Dolby Atmos filling the room with immersive spatial sound, now continuously tuned to your space with Advanced Room Adaptation. What’s new is context: with more awareness of its surroundings, Alexa can help in real time—explaining the rules on a board game box you hold up, recognizing a box of cereal to help you reorder it, or letting you check in on the room from the Alexa app while you’re away.

The original Echo Studio without the camera is $219.99, while the new model is available today at $249.99.

Echo Time smart bedside clock

The new Echo Time has a display that gradually brightens to mimic a sunrise as your alarm time approaches, and a sleep sensor provides the option of waking you when you’re in a lighter sleep phase.

Echo Time is purpose-built for the bedside—with a customizable display and camera-free design to make waking up and winding down effortless. Make it yours with hundreds of clock faces to choose from—including everything from analog and modern to playful designs and even your favorite sports teams. Its new sleep sensing technology, powered by Omnisense, can sense when you’re in lighter sleep and wakes you within 10 to 60 minutes of your scheduled alarm, no wearable device required. As your alarm approaches, the display gradually brightens to mimic a natural sunrise and the tone builds gently to help ease you awake.

The standard model is available today for $199.99, with a kids version again at $10 more with a year of Kids+ included.

Alexa Photo Frame

	

A new photo frame syncs to Amazon Photos to show the latest photos as you take them, with the ability to ask Alexa to find the photos you want to display.

Most of the photos we love never leave our phones. The Alexa Photo Frame changes that—pairing the timeless elegance of a traditional frame with the intelligence of Alexa, so your best memories are always on display. It’s the first photo frame with Alexa built in, and it works effortlessly: connect it to Amazon Photos and your pictures sync automatically, with new ones appearing as they’re taken. Alexa intelligently surfaces the shots worth seeing—the ones where you’re smiling, in the right season—and skips the screenshots and clutter. Just ask to see photos of a favorite person, pet, or trip, or swipe through right on the 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen, where every picture looks crisp and vibrant from any angle.

The Alexa Photo Frame is available today for $199.99 in black or $229 in real birch or walnut.

Echo Show 16

Finally, the tablet-like Echo Show 15 has been upgraded to offer 10% more viewing area on a 16-inch screen in a thinner device with a nanomatte anti-reflective option. Like Apple’s HomeView, there are options for placing on a countertop via an iMac-like stand or mounting on a wall.

The all-new Echo Show 16 is our most advanced display yet, with 20% more power for interactions that feel fast. The 16-inch high-definition screen is nearly 40% thinner with 10% more viewing area, and a new Nanomatte option cuts glare by more than 90% while keeping detail and color razor-sharp. Screen Styles transform it into whatever your home needs most—a family organizer with color-coded calendars, chores, and meal plans; a digital photo frame; or a smart home dashboard with the new Alexa Home Map, showing every light, lock, thermostat, and camera right where it lives in your home. Plus, it has the full Fire TV experience, built in. Echo Show 16 has our best-ever camera on an Echo Show, featuring the widest field of view, auto-framing that keeps everyone in view, and—for the first time—night vision, so you can check in with Live View day or night.

The Echo Show 16 is available for pre-order today at $499.99 or $569.99 with the nanomatte screen. Availability hasn’t yet been confirmed, with the company simply saying that it will begin shipping “later this year.”

title: Android 17-based Redmagic OS 12 gets closer to a global release
snippet: The global rollout schedule is still a bit of a mystery, but we at least know which Redmagic devices are getting the Redmagic OS 12 Android 17 upgrade. more…
fullText:
The global rollout schedule is still a bit of a mystery, but we at least know which Redmagic devices are getting the Redmagic OS 12 Android 17 upgrade.

Redmagic is updating 8 of its latest devices to Android 17 in China, which began with the launch of the Redmagic 12 Pro+. Redmagic calls its Android 17 skin “Redmagic OS 12,” and the update includes a slew of visual changes, more AI integration, simplified connectivity and file transfer to iPhones, and a bunch of gaming and performance upgrades. Here’s the timeline:

December 2026: Redmagic 11 Pro and Redmagic 11S Pro series

January 2027: Redmagic Gaming Tablet 5 Pro

March 2027: Redmagic 10 Pro series, Redmagic 10S Pro series, Redmagic 11 Air, and Redmagic eSports Tablet 3 Pro

April 2027: Redmagic 10 Air

While these are technically the Chinese upgrade dates, we expect Redmagic to follow with global availability shortly afterward. Redmagic 12 Pro gets a global release date on November 3, 2026, so a global version of Redmagic OS 12 is already finished and just needs to be ported to these other devices.

As is the case with many Android 17 updates, this one focuses on a visual redesign that includes more Liquid Glass-inspired design, including a giant lockscreen clock and new lockscreen customizations. A Dynamic Island-like feature called AI Magic Island adorns the status bar and expands for actionable notifications like music playback, ride-hailing, and more, presumably using Android 17’s Live Updates feature.

	

The MORA AI companion is a new VTuber-like AI assistant that’s now built into the phone, and Redmagic is also including new “AI Magic Assistant” automated task executions to go along with it. A refreshed Game Space app is included in the OS update, as well as an Esports Training Arena app with built-in shooting and reaction mini-games, plus the X-Gravity Platform 3.0 update and upgraded live streaming capabilities.

title: Gemini for Android rolls out side panel and settings redesign
snippet: Following the Spark-to-Task update, the Gemini app has now rolled out redesigns of the side panel and settings on Android. more…
fullText:
Following the Spark-to-Task update, the Gemini app has now rolled out redesigns of the side panel and settings on Android.

This revamp starts with Google moving search to the top-right corner. The first item in the list remains New chat, with Library appearing next instead of being located near the bottom. 

To avoid cluttering the navigation drawer while still allowing you to view recent chats, Gemini displays only five items before making use of “More,” which expands the list upon tapping. With an AI Ultra subscription, the full list is as follows: New chat, Library, Images, Scheduled, Daily brief, Customize, Students, Videos, and Gems.

Old vs. new

	

Meanwhile, the Gemini app is revamping settings. Instead of having preferences split between the account menu and “Gemini Settings,” Google has consolidated everything into one page. The account menu is now just for switching accounts, leaving Feedback, or getting Help.

The “Settings” page starts with Manage account and Usage limits. Under Preferences, you’ll find Notifications, Personal Intelligence, Avatar, Task settings, Theme (new), Skills, Voice, Media, Device controls, Cart and orders, and Gemini Notebook. There are two other sections:

Data & privacy: Import memory, Contact info from your devices, Gemini Apps Activity, Your public links, and Privacy Help Hub.

Get support: Help, Report a problem, About, and Updates.

The updated side panel and settings rolled out to iOS, macOS, and the web app last week with the launch of Gemini 4 Argon. We’re now seeing wide availability on Android following a server-side update.

A surge of online reports indicates that some users are experiencing a recent increase in battery drain on their Pixel Watch, by as much as 20% every few hours.

Sometimes new software introduces extra stress on device batteries. New processes can take a toll on phone or smartwatch energy at a higher cost than expected, and that might be what’s happening with some Pixel Watch users.

It’s nowhere near a definitive trend, but it’s intriguing to see several new posts on Reddit pop up with the same complaint – their Pixel Watch’s battery is draining faster than normal (via Android Authority). One post has 65 comments, with a healthy number sharing the same concern. One user wrote that their Pixel Watch 2 is getting 12 hours of use on a full charge, instead of the normal 48 hours with AOD off.

The other user claims their Pixel Watch 4 now lasts less than a day. Their normal usage reportedly gets them up to 2.5 days. That’s high for the Pixel Watch 4, but it’s not unheard of. Both of these users dropping by 12 or 24 hours from one charge isn’t nothing.

	
	

Sporadic comments echo the same situation, but many report they haven’t noticed a difference. Timing isn’t entirely consistent across comments, either. Some say they started seeing the issue a few days ago, while others say this happened to them a while back.

Still, it might indicate a recent software update is to blame. Google’s recent September 2026 update reaches the Pixel Watch 2 and newer. It adds “Gemini Personalization,” which Google says leverages past conversations and Google apps like Gmail or Calendar to offer personalized responses. It’s also possible that the battery is affected by the recent Google Health update with automatic activity tracking, but that wouldn’t explain why the Pixel Watch 2 is having an issue.

It’s unclear if that’s playing a factor, but Google has yet to officially acknowledge the issue for these users.

What about you? Is your Pixel Watch suddenly dying in the middle of the day? The comments section is all yours.

title: Google Beam 3D meeting booths will expand access for military families

fullText:
Google announced an expansion of its 3D meeting booths, giving military families access to Google Beam in over 20 locations.

Google Beam, originally Project Starline, has recently expanded in several steps. After becoming available at the corporate level, Google has begun making the 3D video conferencing tech available to users in co-working spaces through its partnership with HP.

Today, Google announced another expansion. Google Beam video booths will be available at 20 USO locations globally. This comes after a pilot program was set up for military members and their families in Poland and Texas.

That’s why we’re partnering with the United Service Organizations (USO) to bring the HP

Dimension with Google Beam video communication solution to 20 USO locations globally,

helping service members bridge this distance. With true-to-life, 3D video communication

technology, families can feel like they are stepping into the same space and connect in an

entirely new way.

The expansion will reach Grafenwöehr, Germany, and Fort Hood, Texas, in addition to those two existing locations for the time being.

	

Google partnered with Kyle Hausmann-Stokes, a filmmaker and veteran, to produce a docuseries that expands on how Google Beam is being used in the military. In total, the series follows four families in For Bliss, Texas, as they get to use the 3D video booths to go beyond traditional video calls.

You can watch the series on Google’s YouTube channel.

title: US government acting illegally over electronic surveillance of its own citizens, say senators
snippet: Two senators with notable expertise in intelligence matters say that the US government is acting illegally over electronic surveillance of its own citizens. They say the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) has permitted intelligence agencies to continue warrantless interception of messages by US citizens despite failing to comply with the administration’s own privacy promise to allow public review of such rulings … more…
fullText:
Two senators with notable expertise in intelligence matters say that the US government is acting illegally over electronic surveillance of its own citizens.

They say the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) has permitted intelligence agencies to continue warrantless interception of messages by US citizens despite failing to comply with the administration’s own privacy promise to allow public review of such rulings …

The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) was supposed to allow interception of communications by agents of foreign powers on US soil. It also put in place safeguards intended to ensure proper oversight. Controversially, however, it has also been used to intercept the communications of American citizens without a warrant under a clause known as Section 702.

That latter power is supposed to be granted for 12 months at a time by FISC. Decisions to renew the authorization should be made public within 180 days. It was last renewed back in March, with a deadline for public review expiring on September 13th. 

As Wired reports, however, that has still not happened.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September […]

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

The report also says that additional oversight through things like internal auditing within the FBI has been abandoned, and it’s no longer possible to track how many times search filters have been used to restrict electronic surveillance to US citizens.

Wyden is the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff formerly chaired the equivalent House committee.

title: You don’t need to believe in a god to get a religious exemption from using AI at work
snippet: David Durman, a University of Kentucky administrator, recently earned a religious exemption from using AI in the workplace.
fullText:
Pope Leo XIV has decried AI as a threat to human dignity, but it’s not just the devoutly faithful who might worry about how AI squares with their beliefs. David Durman, a nontheistic humanist, recently secured a religious exemption from using AI in the workplace.

“Humanism is a collection of beliefs about the human experience and how humans interact with the world,” Durman, a University of Kentucky administrator, told TechCrunch. It centers on “human well-being and flourishing, both individually and collectively … and implores a person to try to improve both their well-being and their flourishing as well as the others around them.”

As he watched AI grow more popular in daily life, Durman sought out the American Humanist Association (AHA) — a nonprofit advancing secular humanism — to investigate how he could gain legal protections against having to use AI at work. He believes that using the technology runs counter to his beliefs.

“The way we become moral actors for ourselves and for others is through the active application of our minds, and the diminishing of that [through AI use] is going to necessarily have a negative impact on our ability to do so,” he said, reflecting on how overreliance on AI might affect critical thinking.

In a statement published by the AHA earlier this week, Durman wrote, “AI is interfering with people’s ability to earn a living, the environmental costs spell disaster for humanity and our planet, and its supplanting and theft of human creativity threaten elements of our culture like art and literature that make society flourish.”

Humanism is not anti-religious, but it tends to appeal to people who are skeptical of a god or other supernatural power yet still seek a scientific and moral framework to ground themselves in.

“Concern about AI and human dignity can run through several different faiths and traditions, whether that’s Catholic teachings, or Universalism, or Humanism, and we want Humanists or nontheists to know that they fall into these categories — that they are also protected by the law at work,” Alexandria Huiskens, staff attorney at the AHA, told TechCrunch.

Durman is the first humanist to secure workplace accommodations that allow him to abstain from AI use, and one of the first people to publicly discuss their pursuit of these protections. He was inspired to seek them when he read that Erin Maus, a Unitarian Universalist and software engineer, was able to secure similar protections for herself.

“For me, this was about me and my convictions,” Durman said. “I’m obviously not trying to tell people how to think or feel … But I do hope that it encourages people who have similar concerns to pursue not necessarily religious exemption, but pursue their concerns to the best of their ability where they feel is the most appropriate.”

University of Kentucky spokesperson Jay Blanton told TechCrunch that the institution reviews requests for religious accommodations on an individual basis, considering the employee’s job responsibilities and the circumstances of the request.

“In this case, the university determined that an accommodation could be provided while allowing the employee to continue performing the essential functions of their position,” Blanton said in a statement. “As technology and job responsibilities evolve, accommodations may be reviewed to ensure they remain reasonable and workable.” 

Maus’ situation is especially unusual, since it has become rare for software engineers to write code without any AI assistance. But in Durman’s administrative role, in which he supports researchers applying for grants, he has not been required to use AI at work. Like many workers across fields, some of his colleagues and leadership have recommended that employees try out these tools, so he sought to secure his exemption now, in case the suggestion becomes a mandate in the future.

“I hope that if [others] have similar feelings, that they feel encouraged to pursue some kind of resolution,” Durman said.

She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. title: Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop
snippet: After months of bombarding mathematicians with a relentless stream of AI-generated results, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he sympathizes with researchers struggling to make sense of it all. But he has no intention of stopping - and hints there could be much more to come from the company's stockpile of discoveries. "I think, on net, the world deserves to understand how the universe works," Altman said during an episode of the Cheeky Pint podcast released Thursday. "But I do have empathy for the method." His comments mark one of the first times the OpenAI chief has directly acknowledged the company's impact on mathematicians, following a strin … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
After months of bombarding mathematicians with a relentless stream of AI-generated results, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he sympathizes with researchers struggling to make sense of it all. But he has no intention of stopping — and hints there could be much more to come from the company’s stockpile of discoveries.

“I think, on net, the world deserves to understand how the universe works,” Altman said during an episode of the Cheeky Pint podcast released Thursday. “But I do have empathy for the method.”

His comments mark one of the first times the OpenAI chief has directly acknowledged the company’s impact on mathematicians, following a string of genuinely impressive AI-generated results whose chaotic, poorly communicated rollouts have left researchers bewildered and struggling to keep up, even amid widespread excitement about AI’s potential as a tool for discovery.

Altman argued that the public’s right to new scientific knowledge “outweighs” the disruption caused by OpenAI’s releases, though he acknowledged the company needs to improve how it communicates its findings. “I feel unequivocal on this point: Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge, and we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery,” he said. “The world deserves that.”

Mathematicians speaking to The Verge have repeatedly criticized OpenAI for how it announces its results, citing inadequate attribution, little context, and insufficient verification. Researchers say this has left them doing the painstaking work of checking and making sense of their findings even as the company presses ahead with more. This month alone, OpenAI has released hundreds of mathematical results, often with little more than brief writeups that researchers have described as poorly written and hard to follow.

Yet OpenAI is now facing criticism for doing precisely what Altman says it should not be: sitting on potentially significant findings. Mathematicians and scientists speaking to The Verge this week said they are frustrated by what they see as OpenAI’s gatekeeping of research, following the announcement of three major breakthroughs in mathematics, physics, and computer science. Details for one of the claimed results — involving Yang-Mills theory, the mathematical foundations of modern particle physics — have not been released publicly. OpenAI says it is due to the recommendations of a hand-picked group of experts it consulted on how best to release it. The practice runs directly counter to the advice of a previous group of mathematicians the company consulted, but forms part of what the company says is a new approach to communicating its findings.

On the podcast, Altman hints that OpenAI is sitting on many more mathematical discoveries than it has made public, too. Asked whether the company has more than the hundreds of proofs they have already released, Altman replied: “We do. Of course.”

Altman also acknowledged that OpenAI’s pursuit of mathematical problems did “get out of control” for a short period of time, but said that was deliberate and necessary to probe the limits of its AI models. He described an internal Slack channel called “Model Name-Hold My Beer,” where employees “were just throwing that at the hardest problems they could” to see how the models would perform.

Altman also estimated that OpenAI has spent in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars tackling mathematical problems, including around $10 million — “maybe a little more” — on its Navier-Stokes solution, one of mathematics’s legendary Millennium Prize problems. The spending offers a glimpse of the vast resources AI labs are bringing to bear on scientific problems, raising concerns among researchers that they may be priced out of their own fields.

It looks like mathematicians and other researchers hoping for a breather may be out of luck.

title: Maine’s data center revolt will decide who controls the Senate
snippet: Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, was midway through defending her record during the final debate of the midterms when an audience member cut her short. "I'm terrified," a man shouted. "AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our water." Collins brushed off the outburst, tying the man to her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. But the fear echoing through the auditorium wasn't so easily dismissed. Just days before voters head to the polls, the rapid expansion of resource-hungry data centers has exploded into one of Maine's most volatile campaign issues. Maine drew national headlines in April when the state Le … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, was midway through defending her record during the final debate of the midterms when an audience member cut her short.

“I’m terrified,” a man shouted. “AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our water.” Collins brushed off the outburst, tying the man to her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. But the fear echoing through the auditorium wasn’t so easily dismissed. Just days before voters head to the polls, the rapid expansion of resource-hungry data centers has exploded into one of Maine’s most volatile campaign issues.

Maine drew national headlines in April when the state Legislature passed what would have been the nation’s first statewide moratorium on large data centers — had Gov. Janet Mills not vetoed the bill 10 days later. But the fight hasn’t slowed down, with towns across the state adopting temporary moratoriums or putting the question of data center expansion to voters this November. In a September poll of Mainers by UMass Lowell and YouGov, 76 percent of respondents said they oppose building a data center in their community, with 58 percent strongly opposed.

Maine’s hotly contested Senate race is set to be the most expensive Senate race per capita that the US has ever seen, with Democrats spending a projected $81 million and Republicans $114 million. Much of that campaign cash has come from the very industry Mainers and rural voters across the country have been fighting for more than a year. The outcome of the race will help determine which party controls the Senate and help shape federal data center and AI policy, impacting data center construction not just for Maine residents, but for the entire country.

Cheap land, rich water

Maine and other rural states are becoming prime targets for new data centers. While cities run short on land and power, Maine has abundant cheap land, vacant industrial mills and buildings, and ample access to water, thanks to its numerous rivers and waterways. Recognizing the high stakes, major tech companies and private equity firms tied to data centers and AI have invested millions in the midterms to win over skeptical locals.

The issue has sparked fierce local debate, leading towns and cities across the state to enact temporary bans this summer.

Molly White, the researcher, writer, and software engineer behind Tech Influence Watch, says that voters are paying a lot of attention to the issue because they connect data centers to rising costs for utilities. As White points out, many Mainers are also already feeling the pinch due to record-high heating oil costs this fall, and “they’re now looking at an election where the question is, is this candidate going to invite a data center to move in next door, and then my electricity prices go up, or the knock-on effects are going to hurt me even more when I’m already in very dire straits?” she said.

White launched her site in 2024 to track crypto spending in political races, but has since expanded it to monitor AI and Big Tech investments. White says the playbook that AI and data center backers are using in the midterms is very similar to the one the cryptocurrency industry used in 2024.

“There’s a lot going on in this election,” White says, “but I do think it has been a big issue in Maine and across the country, where you’ll go to a political event, you’ll see people asking questions of candidates, and AI keeps coming up. Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.”

“Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.”

— Molly White

Data center developers and their political allies often sell rural Maine communities on long-term job creation — a promise economists say rarely materializes. In reality, economic research indicates that most data centers create virtually no net employment once construction is complete.

Historically, Maine’s industry has centered around lumber and timber, shipbuilding, commercial fishing, textiles, and pulp and paper manufacturing. The timber industry contributed around $8.3 billion to Maine’s economy in 2024, but Donald Trump’s tariffs and rising operating costs have hit it hard, resulting in mill closures and layoffs.

Mark Brewer, who chairs the political science department at the University of Maine, says Maine’s history complicates the debate. These former mill towns jump at the chance to rebuild their local tax bases and infrastructure, but past boom-and-bust cycles make residents cautious.

“Maine has a long history of extractive industries providing jobs,” Brewer says, which allowed Mainers to tolerate these industries despite the state’s environmental focus. With data centers thus far, he says, “the jobs part of it’s not there. It’s one thing to put up with a paper mill that’s employing three shifts of 1,000 workers, right? Data centers aren’t doing that.”

For many rural Mainers, the question is not only whether a data center will bring jobs back, but whether to trust the companies promising them or the government helping make the deal, said Nicholas Jacobs, the director of the Public Policy Lab at Colby College in Maine. These residents say they’re concerned about the opaque ownership of these data centers, limited long-term employment, and the risk of wealth being extracted from rural communities.

Tech millions fuel Collins’ reelection war chest

Tech and AI interests see an ally in Susan Collins, the 73-year-old Republican chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Like most congressional Republicans, she has largely supported data centers and AI, though she has said she believes data centers should be evaluated on an individual basis. Collins has even used her position as head of the Appropriations Committee to secure $6.2 million in federal funding for a high-performance computing hub data center in central Maine, which is designed to bolster localized AI and biotech research. Her stance has brought in a tremendous amount of campaign donations from Big Tech, AI, and data center donors for her reelection bid.

Collins’ individual donors include Alex Karp, the cofounder and CEO of Palantir; Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz of VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, which heavily backs data centers; and others from Google, Meta, and Microsoft. According to White’s donation tracker, Collins has received $325,644 from AI and crypto donors. Nearly 100 billionaires have donated to Collins’ reelection bid in some form or another.

“It’s one thing to put up with a paper mill that’s employing three shifts of 1,000 workers, right? Data centers aren’t doing that.”

— Mark Brewer

Super PACs like the Republican Senate Leadership Fund dumped nearly $42 million into ads across Maine. Elon Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund this summer, and has spent around $450 million of his own money to support Republicans in the midterms. Musk’s America PAC has spent around $2.1 million in Maine. Pine Tree Results PAC, to which Collins and her husband have personal ties, put $29.1 million into the race to support her. Stephen Schwarzman from Blackstone has donated $2 million this year to Pine Tree Results.

A recent FEC report flagged by the Maine Newsroom shows that Musk’s corporate SpaceX PAC gave $55,000 to Collins’ Victory Committee in August and another $50,000 to the Pine Tree Results PAC.

The campaign and PAC money appears to flow in support of just one candidate, too. Collins’ opponent Troy Jackson only recently filed his FEC paperwork, which shows no obvious data center, AI, or Big Tech ties, though it does show at least four billionaire donors. However, Jackson’s stance is similar to Collins’, and he focuses largely on putting guardrails in place for AI and data center development. He has said he wants to ensure union jobs for the buildout and maintenance of data centers in the state.

Collins’ ties to data centers don’t stop with her donors. Her family has actual stakes in the AI boom. Earlier this month, Forbes ranked Collins’ household fifth in the Senate for AI- and data center-linked investments, with an estimated $300,000 to $800,000 held in her husband Thomas Daffron’s name.

Daffron is a former lobbyist and was paid consulting fees in 2025 by the lobbying firm of Scott Reed. Reed chairs Pine Tree Results, the super PAC with close ties to Collins. And according to American Journal News and The New York Times, Reed’s firm lobbied for a developer that has built data centers in Maine. Collins’ financial disclosure shows that she and her husband hold assets worth anywhere from $4 million to $10 million.

Jackson, who started as a logger before he was elected to the state Senate, has most recently earned money from consulting, and he and his wife hold assets worth anywhere from $147,000 to $430,000. He doesn’t have any reported financial ties to data centers, AI, or Big Tech interests.

Outside money and extractive boom-and-bust fears fuel backlash

Billionaire influence tends to spark partisan backlash, White notes, adding that Mainers resent wealthy outsiders trying to buy their votes. Jacobs agrees, noting that many Maine voters harbor a deep, long-standing skepticism toward anyone from “away” looking to exploit local resources.

“Rural wealth exists, but it is extracted out of the community, and that’s the game of rural living,” Jacobs says. “You harvest your timber; you send it away. You harvest your crops; you send them away. It’s extractive, but there’s a fine line between an extractive economy and an exploitive economy. And so I do think that there is a history and maybe even a culture of wariness towards that form of exploitation.”

Brewer says he is skeptical that the huge amount of campaign spending will sway rural voters’ views about data centers. If anything, voters may punish Collins for her ties to Elon Musk and other unpopular tech billionaires.

“Rural wealth exists, but it is extracted out of the community, and that’s the game of rural living.”

— Nicholas Jacobs

Much of the campaign spending from the super PACS with a vested interest in data centers and AI has flooded the airwaves and mailboxes with hostile attack ads, Jacobs and Brewer note. With broadcast television inventory completely sold out, campaigns have shifted money into radio, social media, and direct mail. The sheer volume has pushed voters past their breaking point, Brewer says, calling the contest “the most negative race” he has tracked in 25 years of observing Maine politics.

According to a recent Maine Monitor report, as of mid-October, $54 million has been spent or committed for negative attack ads, and nearly all of it is coming from outside PACs financed by Big Tech and data center supporters, not the candidates’ campaigns. While no ads have focused specifically on Collins’ support for data centers and AI, some have targeted her ties to Big Tech, billionaires, and data centers through her husband. The National Republican Senatorial Committee tried to tie Troy Jackson to Senate Democrats’ opposition to the Husted legislation in September in a press release.

“That is where the overwhelming amount of money is going,” Jacobs says about the attack ads. “It’s ads, and then paying consultants to write the ads, polling, paying the consultants to do the polls, right? The worst case is that it tarnishes the image of democracy in voters’ minds, and I think that is the most significant consequence beyond any quid pro quo relationship.”

As Jacobs notes, many Maine voters, especially independents, are conflicted about data center investment in the state. They are deeply attached to their community and wary of outsiders changing it, while also worried their children won’t be able to afford to stay or find good jobs without the influx of tech money.

“I think many people throughout Maine worry about the future and whether or not their children will be able to afford to live there,” he says. “Whether there will be jobs. Both of these things are true … Data centers just seem to be this symbolic flashpoint of that tension in rural living.”

title: Here’s Why You’re About to See More Ads in Google’s AI Overviews
snippet: With Google now injecting “sponsored” links directly into AI follow-up queries, traffic to online publishers will suffer even more.
fullText:
If you happened to listen to Alphabet’s quarterly earnings call on Wednesday, you might have heard that searches are up, but ad revenue is down. According to Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler, search ad revenue growth slowed in the third quarter of 2026 because user queries are migrating to AI Overviews and AI Mode, which suffer from “lower monetization.”

You actually know how this works. When you type a question into Google, a summarized AI response often appears immediately, reducing the classic ad-clicking behavior further down on the page, which generates Google’s core revenue.

Now, the tech giant is expanding how and where we see ads when using AI Mode during searches. Google is scaling ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries (including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore), with plans to launch in Brazil, Mexico and the UK later this year. 

			

More from CNET

In the US, Google is launching what it calls “multiturn ads,” allowing ads to appear directly within follow-up queries in AI Mode when a search or conversation has “commercial relevance.” Take, for example, if you start a search with “How does a smart fridge work,” and follow up with “What are the best-selling smart fridges?” You could then see refrigerator ads in sections labeled “sponsored.”

Google said that “multiturn ads” can better target what a user wants in a product because AI Mode gathers more information during a back-and-forth conversation. Ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, not just after follow-up questions, and sometimes ads won’t appear at all if there doesn’t appear to be purchase intent, according to Google.

But as Google relies more on AI Mode and AI Overview, there’ll be less reason to click on content links “below the fold,” meaning content that sits out of view until a reader scrolls down a web page. 

Lily Ray, a well-known SEO expert and founder of Algorythmic, told CNET that it’s going to become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers and articles you want to read directly from a website. “You’ll have to dig deeper and look outside of Google’s products,” Ray said via email. 

According to Ray, Google’s AI tools aren’t designed to give you the exact link you’re looking for. Still, you don’t have to rely on AI Mode or AI Overviews to get search results. You can also scroll down to the search results the old-fashioned way or use a web filter to use Google as a list of links. She also recommends setting up your favorite publications as “preferred sources” (instructions here) so you can see more of those pages cited in your personalized results.

“Unless you’re satisfied with AI answers directly on Google, you’re going to need to start evolving your own search behavior to find the websites you’re looking for,” Ray said. 

AI, advertising and traffic 

Google is still the largest search engine in the world, accounting for nearly 90% of the global search engine market. In fact, the company said its year-over-year query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest over the past five years.

But beginning with the launch of AI Overviews in May 2024, Google’s reliance on AI has slowed advertising. 

The impact has been even more devastating for online publishers — ranging from major newspapers and digital media sites to brands and trade associations — driving an unprecedented decline in website traffic. AI Overviews now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a corresponding 61% drop in raw traffic volume to other pages. Google is effectively scraping publisher information, summarizing it and satisfying the user before they leave the search results page. That’s why it’s often referred to as the “zero-click” crisis.

“AI Mode and AI Overviews answer questions directly in Google’s interface, so there’s less reason for people to click on publishers,” Ray said. 

AI Overviews are summary boxes at the top of a traditional search results page, while AI Mode is a conversational interface designed for ongoing dialogue and research. You can access AI Mode directly by selecting the AI Mode button at the far right of the search bar on the Google home page, or by selecting AI Mode in the horizontal menu near the top of other Google pages.

When you use AI Mode, you won’t get an AI Overview or a long list of links to other websites offering more information. Instead, AI Mode provides “more advanced reasoning and ways of interacting” with a conversational approach. For instance, if I use AI Mode and ask, “Where can I see the northern lights?” I get a map and a list of various locations with pros and cons for each. In regular search mode, I get an AI Overview at the top and, below that, pages of links to websites related to my query.

Ray said that with more ads, there’s going to be an even greater decline in organic click-through rates — in publishing speak, that’s the percentage of people who actually click on a natural, nonpaid search engine result, out of the total number of people who simply saw the headline on the page. Not only will the AI text answer your question, but Google will now aggressively route you toward advertisers rather than publisher links.

“Like many things in Google Search, it means that if you’re not participating in Google Ads, it’s going to be harder and harder to get that traffic organically,” said Ray.

According to Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler, search ad revenue growth slowed in the third quarter of 2026 because user queries are migrating to AI Overviews and AI Mode, which suffer from “lower monetization.”

You actually know how this works. When you type a question into Google, a summarized AI response often appears immediately, reducing the classic ad-clicking behavior further down on the page, which generates Google’s core revenue.

snippet: Waymo announced today that when it launches a robotaxi service in Tokyo in 2027, it will use Toyota bZ4X electric vehicles that are assembled in Japan. fullText:
Andrew J. Hawkins

 

is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Waymo announced today that when it launches a robotaxi service in Tokyo in 2027, it will use Toyota bZ4X electric vehicles that are assembled in Japan. The news builds on the strategic partnership between Waymo and Toyota which was first announced in April 2025.

The robotaxis will be built entirely under one roof at Toyota’s Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan. Instead of building regular cars and modifying them later, the factory will install Waymo’s self-driving sensors and computers right on the assembly line as each car is made.

A team-up between the world’s largest automaker and the world’s leader in autonomous driving obviously has huge implications. Currently, Waymo uses two vehicle models on the road today — the Jaguar I-Pace and Zeekr RT — with a third based on the Hyundai Ioniq 5 set to deploy soon. By adding the bZ4X, Waymo is attempting to prove that its autonomous driving technology is compatible with a wide range of vehicle types. Waymo has long positioned itself as a software and systems supplier — the “Waymo Driver” — rather than an automaker.

A team-up between the world’s largest automaker and the world’s leader in autonomous driving obviously has huge implications

This also represents a shift in terms of how Waymo acquires and modifies the vehicles that end up in its fleet. Up until now, the company was doing things the hard way by buying a finished car from a factory, shipping it to a separate facility, and retrofitting it with sensors, computers, and extra wiring. The decision to build the sensor suite and compute into the bZ4X on Toyota’s own assembly line could help eliminate redundant labor, bespoke brackets, and secondary shipping — and possibly bring down costs for Waymo.

Waymo says it will begin initial testing and validation in Japan starting next year. Following that, the new vehicles will roll out to the United Kingdom, in addition to other international markets, for robotaxi operations.

Waymo also says it is continuing to explore integrating its technology into Toyota vehicles for personally owned autonomous vehicles. And the company is working with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software and mobility spinout, to use Waymo’s operational and safety telemetry to improve road safety across general vehicle fleets and traffic infrastructure.

title: Strava adds Google Gemini integration with personalized workout insights
snippet: Strava expanded its AI integrations with Google Gemini this week, allowing subscribers to get personalized insights based on their workout history. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Strava expanded its AI integrations with Google Gemini this week, allowing subscribers to get personalized insights based on their workout history. Here are the details.

Strava expands AI integration to Gemini

A few months ago, fitness tracking platform Strava launched an integration with Claude using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing users to analyze their workout history and training performance through natural-language conversations with Anthropic’s AI assistant.

MCP is an open standard (created by Anthropic and later donated to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation) that allows AI assistants to connect to external apps and services to access information and perform tasks on behalf of users.

This week, Strava announced an expansion of its AI integrations, bringing similar capabilities to Google Gemini.

As the company explained, Strava subscribers “who connect Strava directly to Gemini will get more contextual and personalized answers grounded in their activity history.” The company added that the integration is entirely optional and read-only

From the announcement:

Once connected, users can ask Gemini things such as:

“Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?” See what’s different in your volume, consistency, and mix of sports, without scrolling through months of activities.

“Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?” Understand how your effort played out, mile by mile.

“How is my strength training impacting my running?”Synthesize trends across any sports you do on Strava.

And with our most recent update, users can also ask:

“What’s my fastest 10K this year vs. all time?” Compare your best efforts side by side, with the date and activity behind each, to see how far you’ve come and what’s still in reach. 

“How much did the heat slow me down on Saturday’s long run?” Work out whether it was your legs or the forecast. The temperature, humidity, wind, and conditions from your activity are now part of the picture.

“How long is my longest running streak on Strava?” Check your current and longest streaks, by sport, and when your current one started, so you know where you stand before the day is over. Or ask, “How long is my run streak?”

The rollout will be limited to the US at first, with the integration available to Strava subscribers regardless of their Gemini plan. Strava has not announced when it might expand to other countries.

title: Reddit Is Adding ‘For You’ and ‘Following’ Feeds
snippet: The new feeds, similar to those used on TikTok, are rolling out worldwide.
fullText:
Reddit is giving users new ways to sift through its billions of posts. The move follows recent platform changes that eliminated RSS feeds and limited access to the site’s classic desktop layout, Old Reddit.

In a blog post published on Wednesday, Reddit says it will introduce For You and Following tabs, similar to those used on TikTok. The new tabs will roll out to Reddit users worldwide over the next few weeks.

The two feeds will work differently. For You is a discovery feed that recommends posts from subreddits you follow, but adds posts the algorithm believes will relate to your interests. The Following tab is made up strictly of posts from subreddits you’ve already joined. Switching between them might give you a choice between a broader view of what’s on Reddit and one made up only of what you’ve curated for yourself as your interests.

			

More from CNET

The two new feeds, the company said, are part of its experiments to help people “more intentionally explore Reddit.”

User pushback against Reddit’s previous platform changes highlights a growing frustration with the site’s design evolution. These updates target RSS feeds, third-party API access, and Old Reddit availability, features long favored by users seeking alternatives to the default interface.

To keep browsing post archives, external apps must now transition to Reddit’s official developer platform or risk losing access entirely. Reddit reports that it is currently helping migrate roughly 14,000 apps to the new framework.

According to the company, the stricter policies are a necessary response to the rise of AI-driven bot traffic, which has surged dramatically and strained server infrastructure.

title: Apple’s best MacBook Pro decision this week had nothing to do with touch
snippet: Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pro brings plenty of welcome upgrades, but one of the best things about this week’s launch is what the company decided not to change. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pro brings plenty of welcome upgrades, but one of the best things about this week’s launch is what the company decided not to change.

Apple’s decision to keep the old Macs around feels like a welcome glitch in the system

Was I aching for a touchscreen Mac? Not particularly. But I can see how useful it might be for a great deal of users, and I’m happy that their day has finally come. Or will come, starting November 6.

But I’ve been aching for a new Mac. Though my 2023 M2 Pro 16-inch MacBook Pro is still a great machine, its 16GB of RAM is starting to feel a bit cramped. Past me knew this was a mistake.

With the prospect of a revamped MacBook Pro just around the corner, I spent the past few weeks excited about the possibility of biting the bullet and splurging for a new one, even though there had been very conflicting rumors about which chips it would pack.

Although in my heart of hearts I had acquiesced to the idea that the new touchscreen MacBook Pro would get the same chips as the current non-touchscreen line, I was also holding on to the hope that Apple would throw in some performance gains to sweeten the rumored $400 premium deal it would carry.

Right? Right?

Well, no.

Performance-wise, the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is identical to the non-touchscreen models, though there is a case to be made that its redesigned thermal system could make it run faster despite using the same chip, though the changes appear to be aimed more at keeping the display cool than improving heat dissipation. Time, and reviews, will tell.

Which makes Apple’s decision to keep the non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro for sale all that more welcome and unexpected.

Even when Apple introduced the Touch Bar back in 2016, the only non-Touch Bar option left was the entry-level 13-inch MacBook Pro. If you wanted a more powerful Mac or a 15-inch model, you had to get with the program and pony up the extra $300 for the 13-inch model with Touch Bar, or $400 for the redesigned 15-inch model.

Yes, there is plenty new with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Tandem OLED display, improved thermal performance, thinner, lighter design, slimmer bezels, redesigned audio system, Dynamic Island (debatable for some, I know), and even the return of the glowing Apple logo (woo!) on the lid are all welcome additions. Oh yeah, and “it has touch as well.”

Put all of that together, and the $400 premium is arguably not that unreasonable.

But if, like me, these improvements feel secondary to the performance boost you’re prioritizing for this particular upgrade, getting those same specs for effectively $400 less (or using those $400 for better specs!) feels like a pretty great deal for all parties involved, future me included.

Will future me have preferred that I wait for the M7 generation? Possibly. But then again, waiting for the perfect moment to upgrade is what got me into this situation in the first place, recent price hikes and all.

title: Android 17 is on 1% of devices after four months, Android 16 on over 25%
snippet: Google has updated its Android distribution numbers with the latest update showing that Android 17 is on just 1% of devices, while Android 16 now makes up the biggest slice of the pie. more…
fullText:
Google has updated its Android distribution numbers with the latest update showing that Android 17 is on just 1% of devices, while Android 16 now makes up the biggest slice of the pie. 

Updated as of October 19, Google’s latest Android distribution numbers offer a peek into the rollout speed of Android 17. Having released to Pixel phones in June, the update has been available for roughly four months. 

At this point, though, Android 17 makes up just 1% of active Android devices, Google’s data shows.

That’s compared to over 25% for Android 16, which released last year. Android 16 was on 7.5% of devices in Google’s last update in December 2025/January 2026, which landed several months after Google released the update. The timing here requires context, as major players like Samsung have only started widely rolling out their Android 17 updates in the past few weeks and are very unlikely to be included in this 1%.

	

The growth of Android 16 is pretty impressive, too, as older versions tend to be still be more widely in use at this point in the schedule, but Android 16 has managed to consolidate quite a bit. 

Google dropped Android 5 (Lollipop) from its data with this update, with Android 5.1 making up just 0.2% of active devices. Android 11, for reasons unclear, still holds over 10%, while Android 12 has dropped to 9.6%. Android 11 has had a higher share in the past few updates.

title: Alphabet reports Q3 2026 revenue of $127.6 billion
snippet: Alphabet today announced Q3 2026 earnings with $127.6 billion in revenue. These numbers range from July to September. more…
fullText:
Alphabet today announced Q3 2026 earnings with $127.6 billion in revenue. These numbers range from July to September.

Revenue is up 25% from $102.3 billion in Q3 2025, with operating income at $40.58 billion and net income of $26.17 billion for this quarter (versus $34.9 billion a year ago). For comparison, Alphabet reported $119.8 billion in revenue and $112.1 billion in net income last quarter.

We had a strong quarter and are now on a half-trillion dollar revenue run rate. Our deep full stack approach is driving momentum across the business, with Alphabet revenues growing 25% year-over year.

Our AI investments are driving overall Search query growth, including commercial queries. In fact, our year-overyear query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.

Google Cloud revenues grew 103%, powered by huge demand for our AI infrastructure and AI solutions. We’re also seeing strong demand for our TPU systems across a wide range of customers.

Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon are now leading at the frontier. Overall, our first-party model APIs are now processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute, more than four times what we processed a year ago.

On top of that, the Gemini app has reached one billion users—making it the fastest-growing product in Google’s history—and we surpassed 150 million YouTube Music and Premium subscribers globally, including trials.

We’re excited by the range of big opportunities ahead of us.”

Sundar Pichai, CEO

In Q3 2026, YouTube ad revenue was $11.2 billion (versus $10.26 billion a year ago), while Cloud reported $30.71 billion (compared to $15.16 billion).

“Google subscriptions, platforms, and devices” — which includes hardware, Play Store, and non-advertising YouTube revenues — reported $14.29 billion, compared to $12.87 billion the same quarter last year.

	

“Other Bets” continues to lose money. It reported $372 million in revenue compared to $344 million in Q3 of 2025. It lost $2.04 billion compared to $1.4 billion in the same quarter of last year.

title: Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform
snippet: Google today announced the Connected Apps Platform as a “unified way for more app developers to bring their capabilities directly into Gemini and Search.” more…
fullText:
Google today announced the Connected Apps Platform as a “unified way for more app developers to bring their capabilities directly into Gemini and Search.”

Existing third-party Connected Apps let you access Adobe, Dropbox, Instacart, OpenTable, Ticketmaster, and other services — now numbering over 50 — from the Gemini app. Google also announced a new Calm integration that will be available in the coming weeks. These @-integrations join first-party offerings like Google Workspace, Photos, and YouTube. To date, the creation process has required working closely with Google. 

Google is now expanding availability on multiple fronts, starting with the Connected Apps Platform. It’s billed as a way to “build once and reach high-intent users.” Developers need to have a cloud-hosted MCP server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs. They then register, test, and submit their Connected Apps using the new Google Connected Console. This new website lets them track traffic, latency, and error rates, as well as control brand identity.

In addition to the Gemini app, Google will soon make existing Connected Apps available in Search. Developers can “choose whether [their app] will go live in Search, the Gemini app, or both.” As part of the recent redesign, the Gemini app gained a new Customize page.

	

Developers can sign up for the preview at developers.google.com/connected-apps. Google is opening up access in phases over the coming months.

title: Samsung can’t decide between a larger Galaxy Z Fold 9 or one with worse specs, and neither can I
snippet: Following a smash hit in the smaller and wider Galaxy Z Fold 8, Samsung is obviously weighing its options behind the scenes when it comes to sequels. According to one leaker, the company is currently deciding between adding another Galaxy Z Fold 9 with a larger display, or one with lesser specs, and I can’t decide which one I want to see either. more…
fullText:
Following a smash hit in the smaller and wider Galaxy Z Fold 8, Samsung is obviously weighing its options behind the scenes when it comes to sequels. According to one leaker, the company is currently deciding between adding another Galaxy Z Fold 9 with a larger display, or one with lesser specs, and I can’t decide which one I want to see either.

Leaker Lanzuk on Naver says that Samsung is adding more options to the Galaxy Z Fold 9 lineup next year after the Galaxy Z Fold 8 garnered “much better response than expected” (translated). It’s all-but-official that Samsung is expanding the lineup – we’ve heard this repeatedly at this point – but exactly what joins the lineup remains unclear.

This latest rumor suggests two possibilities. 

The first is a larger version of the Galaxy Z Fold 8, a “Galaxy Z Fold 9 Plus,” the leaker suggests. This wouldn’t be an Ultra device, but rather would share the same wide form factor as the standard Fold 9, just with a larger pair of displays.

	

The other option is a “Galaxy Z Fold 9 FE” which would downgrade the specs to achieve a lower price point. Samsung tried this with the Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE to essentially no success, but the company’s cuts on that device were far from compelling on a form factor that was already in decline.

Samsung is said to be testing both form factors and “a decision will be made soon,” but only one of the two would move to production and a full release. 

9to5Google’s Take

Personally, I’m split here. I’ve been using the Galaxy Z Fold 8 as my daily smartphone since its launch, and the size is certainly one of its most attractive features. On the one hand, I’d love to have a larger version for better media consumption and multitasking, but I also think Samsung would run into diminishing returns with a larger size. The wider form factor wouldn’t scale nicely to a larger size too, I think.

Meanwhile, a more affordable version seems like a clear win. This form factor has so clearly resonated with customers, and having an option that makes strategic cuts to hit a price of say, $1,400, would be a home run. However, given Samsung’s existing struggles with profitability amid RAMageddon and ever-rising prices, that also feels unrealistic.

I’m very torn on which would be the better option. Which one would you prefer?

title: Apple and OpenAI trade secrets lawsuit now has an official trial date
snippet: Judge Edward Davila today formally established the schedule for Apple’s trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, including a trial date. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Judge Edward Davila today formally established the schedule for Apple’s trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, including a trial date. Here are the details.

Apple and OpenAI set for July 2027 trial

A couple of weeks ago, during an October 14 case management conference, Judge Edward Davila instructed Apple and the defendants to agree on a proposed schedule for the lawsuit, working toward a tentative trial date of July 19, 2027.

The parties were given until October 23 to submit their proposed schedule, which the judge has now formally established.

As we’ve been covering since July, Apple filed this lawsuit accusing the defendants of improperly accessing or using confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts.

In recent days, Apple scored two procedural wins in its efforts to obtain expedited discovery, with Judge Davila granting the company access to additional documents and information from the defendants ahead of the normal discovery process.

In a case management order issued today, Davila established July 19, 2027, at 9 a.m. as the official trial date, with additional deadlines for discovery, motions, and pretrial proceedings in the meantime.

Here’s the official schedule:

Notably, the schedule includes a June 1 deadline for the lead attorneys on both sides to meet and discuss a potential settlement.

title: iOS 27.2 now available: Here’s everything new for iPhone
snippet: iOS 27.2 is now available to everyone after six weeks of beta testing. The update was released on Monday, bringing multiple new iPhone features. Here’s everything you need to know. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 is now available to everyone after six weeks of beta testing. The update was released on Monday, bringing multiple new iPhone features. Here’s everything you need to know. 

Why iOS 27.2 and not iOS 27.1?

Apple released iOS 27 on September 14, bringing a ton of new iPhone features, including Siri AI. iOS 27.2 entered beta testing just two days later on September 16.

What happened to iOS 27.1? iOS 27.1 was exclusive to the iPhone Duo, which was released last week and shipped with iOS 27.1. With iOS 27.2, the software update paths have converged and all iPhones will be on the same page going forward.

iOS 27.2 new features

New Siri AI features

Siri AI was the big new feature in iOS 27, and iOS 27.2 expands the feature in multiple ways. First, Siri AI is now available in these five languages: 

French

Japanese

Korean

Portuguese

Spanish

Second, iOS 27.2 also adds several new features to Siri AI. From Apple’s release notes: 

Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week

Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List

Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting

Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need

Dual Capture mode for Group FaceTime

In iOS 27, Apple added a new Dual Capture feature for FaceTime that lets you have your front and rear cameras active at the same time. The person on the other end of the call will see you as well as whatever you’re looking at. iOS 27.2 expands this feature to Group FaceTime calls for the first time.

Dual Capture requires an iPhone 17 or later, and everyone on the call needs to be running iOS 27.

Also in iOS 27.2, FaceTime now supports adding a third party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call. 

Apple Podcasts

In Apple Podcasts, the “Up Next” queue has been refreshed with two new dedicated rows: New Episodes and Continue Playing. The New Episodes list shows the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing shows in-progress episodes, organized by most recently played. 

Additionally, episode lists also now use color-matched backgrounds based on the podcast art.

TV app changes 

There are two changes to the TV app included in iOS 27.2. First, the update adds Multiview support to iPhone for the first time. This lets you watch up to four live sports streams simultaneously, including MLS, F1, and MLB. 

The Apple TV app in iOS 27.2 adds support for profiles for the first time. This feature has been available on tvOS for several years, but this is the first time it has come to iPhone.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Suggestions in Messages

Suggestions in Messages, which feature Apple tested in iOS 27 but removed before the update was released, have returned in iOS 27.2. This feature adds quick shortcut buttons to Messages, making it easy to add things to apps like Calendar and Reminders with a single tap. 

Apple Music rebrand 

iOS 27.2 introduces a new brand identity for Apple Music. This includes a new app icon, seen above. There are also various interface tweaks throughout the Music app. For example, the red interface accents are now blue. 

This is part of a larger Apple Music rebrand that the company debuted last week. 

iPhone Duo features

iOS 27.2 adds two new features for iPhone Duo: 

Support for Apple Pencil (USB-C)

Edge Light: add a ring light around the edge of your display to illuminate your face during calls. 

More tidbits

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground. 

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments. They can also display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos. 

The Friends tab in the Games app provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages. 

There are small interface tweaks to the Clock app, including smaller a.m. and p.m. labels. 

iOS 27’s Call Context feature, which surfaces information right on your screen when calling a business, has been expanded to include anniversaries.

Security fixes

iOS 27.2 also includes a ton of security fixes, as Apple outlines on its website. There are security fixes in apps like Mail and Safari, as well as Apple Intelligence, the Neural Engine, and more. 

Wrap up

Have you updated to iOS 27.2 yet? What new features stand out most to you? Let us know down in the comments.
