title: What’s Faster Than an F1 Car? The Data Behind the Race
snippet: For diehard fans and newcomers like me, tech offers deeper insights into the race while helping broadcasters tell a richer story. I went behind the scenes to see how it all comes together.
fullText:
Technology has always been central to Formula One, but it’s playing an increasingly important role in how races are brought to fans around the world.

Ahead of the United States Grand Prix, which ran Friday through Sunday in Austin, Texas, I got a behind-the-scenes look at the on-site production facilities and how data is analyzed and turned into broadcast insights that help viewers – newcomers like me included – better understand the action unfolding on the track.

F1 has surged in popularity in the US in recent years, driven by factors like increased social media exposure, new race destinations and a more personal connection with drivers, thanks in part to Netflix’s hit docuseries Drive to Survive. And with cars reaching speeds of up to 230 miles per hour, it’s easy to see what makes the sport so thrilling.

			

More from CNET

But those cars aren’t just lightning-fast; they’re also data-gathering machines. Each F1 car generates around 1.1 million data points per second from 300 sensors. Technology partners like Amazon Web Services help process and analyze that information, turning complex data into insights that anyone, from casual viewers to die-hard data nerds, can understand and enjoy – including race metrics previously available only to production crews. 

F1 is all about high speeds and even faster data.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Then there are people like me, somewhere in between — intrigued by the F1 frenzy but still learning the rules, technical details and strategies that keep millions of fans invested in every race. That’s where a handful of digital tools can help make sense of the fast-moving action, revealing the stories behind the numbers.

“To know a sport is to love a sport,” said Ruth Buscombe, technical adviser and race strategist at Formula One and AWS motorsports ambassador. “When you look at any kind of relationship you have with something that is a passion, it’s about starting as a novice and then learning about it and falling in love with the details of it. And sports has always been that.” 

Inside the Event Technical Centre, the backbone of F1’s global broadcast

Feeds from the on-track cameras and microphones go through F1’s Event Technical Centre before the footage makes its way on air.F1/AWS

Nestled behind the swanky Paddock Club and team hospitality units sits a white, temporary hangar-like facility called the F1 Event Technical Centre, or ETC. 

This hub is where data from across the circuit is brought together. Dozens of cameras and hundreds of microphones capture the sights and sounds of the race from almost every angle, while each car’s 300 sensors monitor everything from tire pressure to airspeed. For broadcast production, these feeds and data streams are then sent to F1’s Media & Technology Centre in Biggin Hill, UK.

Construction of the tent-like ETC, which spans 375 square meters (about 4,036 square feet), begins 10 days before the race and takes five days to complete. The process includes laying a network of over 58 kilometers (around 36 miles) of fiber-optic cables, as well as data antennas that enable two-way information transfer to and from the cars speeding around the track. 

Up to 28 ultra-high-definition trackside cameras capture the action, alongside cable cams, helicopters, drones, free-roaming cameras and slow-motion cameras. More than 90 cameras are mounted directly on the cars, with up to eight views available from each. The 150 microphones positioned around the circuit capture the quintessential sounds of an F1 race, from the roar of the engines to the screech of the tires (now coming in clear to viewers with Dolby Atmos on Apple TV, along with Dolby Vision).

Inside the ETC, around 140 technical, operations and TV production crew members work side by side, surrounded by glowing switchboards, computer screens and monitors displaying the on-track action, including close-up shots of the cars and sweeping aerial views of the circuit.

The ETC houses around 750 pieces of equipment, according to F1.F1/AWS

In one room, timekeepers track lap times to within one ten-thousandth of a second, with additional timekeepers based at the UK’s Media & Technology Centre. Behind them, teams process and relay data from cameras, audio feeds and car sensors to their headquarters in Europe to support real-time strategy decisions. Sensors positioned around the track every 150 meters also help with vehicle tracking and positioning maps, as well as monitoring potential violations, such as speeding in the pit lane. An operations team at the back ensures the ETC and UK command center are in sync.

In another room, directors decide which shots to use and when to cut to replays or add graphics, which are also handled by team members in this area. A separate crew monitors the team radio, which is delayed by around 20 seconds so they can add subtitles and, importantly, bleep out any swear words.

At the far end of the ETC, a wall of routers and servers transmits the live camera feeds, audio and data to the UK’s Media & Technology Centre. There, production teams turn those feeds into the international broadcast watched by around 1.6 billion viewers.

“We have this really diverse fan base, and we have a complicated story to tell,” said Dean Locke, executive director of broadcast at Formula One. It’s not just the fan base that’s diverse, but also the ways people tune in – whether they’re watching on a big screen, a tablet or a phone.

“The way we develop graphics, the way we develop footage, that is something that we keep in mind,” Locke said. “Is it hitting every single fan?”

Giving fans deeper insights with Track Pulse

Formula One partnered with AWS in 2018, moving much of its computing infrastructure from on-premises data centers to the cloud. AWS also helps F1 refine race strategies, improve digital broadcasts and collect and analyze data, of which there is plenty. 

Now, F1 and AWS are making Track Pulse, a tool the broadcast team has used since 2023, available to fans for the first time this season. 

Track Pulse sifts through vast amounts of data from each car’s sensors to highlight the moments and decisions that can shape a race. From sudden changes in pace to shifting weather conditions to tire strategies, these callouts can help viewers better understand not just what’s happening on track but also why it matters. 

“It’s near impossible to have enough pairs of eyes to monitor all 22 cars at the same time and really pick up on the small details of what’s happening,” said Jerome Descreux, AWS senior engagement manager. That’s why broadcast teams have been using Track Pulse to help determine what to spotlight for viewers. And now, viewers can tap into those insights themselves via F1’s data channel, whether they’re watching in the US through Apple TV or internationally with an F1 TV Pro or Premium subscription. 

Track Pulse can offer more in-depth insights into what’s unfolding on track, giving viewers a heads-up on what to look out for and why.AWS

The interface is a data-rich dashboard with developing “stories,” as they’re called, on the left side, such as when a driver is quickly catching up to another. Track Pulse also displays live team radio transcripts, allowing viewers to peek into the conversations impacting the race. The goal is to distill the endless raw data into elements viewers may be interested in exploring and following.  

For instance, during the 2026 Australian Grand Prix, Track Pulse flagged a moment when George Russell rapidly closed the gap between him and Lewis Hamilton. The tool highlighted this point because of just how quickly Russell was catching up. Track Pulse also noted that Hamilton was using the same tires for an unusually long time, giving fans further insight into the decisions shaping the action on track. 

“We need to make sure that we’re bringing our fans on the journey,” said Formula One IT Director Chris Roberts. “For those people that are really technical, we’re not dulling things down so that it’s a bit boring for them, but also for those fans that are on a learning journey, we’re giving them the information that allows them to understand the sport at different levels.”

Most people might not get the chance to sit trackside, but data feeds for viewers at home can make the action feel closer.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

On the broadcast side, Track Pulse’s AI insights complement the F1 production team’s work, helping them sift through millions of data points to identify key race moments and turn them into digestible insights for people hungry to understand more of the action.

“We originally designed [Track Pulse] to be a producer’s tool,” Locke said. “Then we realized the power of it as a storytelling device. And it could crunch data and create story cards and tell us things that are going on in the races that even an entrenched producer of 20 years wasn’t seeing.”

He added, “Once someone gets into Formula One, they realize how much depth there is, and I think Track Pulse explains it quite well.”

Getting deeper insights with AI  

Insights powered by AWS can help distill the fast-moving action on the track.AWS

AWS also powers around two dozen data-driven F1 Insights, as they’re called, which add real-time analysis to live broadcasts. One example is the Battle Forecast, which estimates how many laps it might take for a chasing car to get close enough to attempt an overtake. The prediction is based on information like track history and projected driver pace, giving viewers a better sense of when the action could heat up.

Tire Performance is another insight that helps fans understand how different driving styles affect tire longevity and how tire condition can influence pit stop timing. And Close to the Wall uses specialized cameras and deep neural network algorithms to track a car’s trajectory in real time and calculate just how close it is to a wall, since even a slight brush at high speeds can affect lap times or damage the car’s carbon-fiber components.

Today, fans can essentially tap into the same data that teams and strategists have long used to gain even the slightest edge over their competitors.

On-screen blurbs can help viewers understand why a team made a particular decision.AWS

“[Teams and strategists] have been doing this for 70 years before anybody at home got to see it,” Buscombe said. “And now, AWS is using the exact same data, doing the exact same math, creating the exact same insights. But rather than it just being a black box where the Formula One teams get to have all the fun, now you, as a fan sitting on your sofa – whether it’s your first race or your 1,000th – you get to see the same kind of data. And those are the F1 insights that pop up on screen.”

Tech and data are set to play an even bigger role in the sport, particularly with AWS now serving as the official AI and cloud computing partner of the FIA, Formula One’s governing body. The partnership could influence everything from race operations to the design of future cars. Running aerodynamic simulations using AWS cloud computing, for instance, allows the FIA to virtually test how air flows around a car without building physical components, which can potentially speed up development.

This past weekend was my first foray into the world of F1, but the combination of technology, data and high-speed racing has already piqued my interest. I may still have plenty to learn, but at least I have some tools to help me make sense of it all.

Editors’ note: Abrar Al-Heeti’s travel costs for the F1 United States Grand Prix in Austin were covered by AWS. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

											Abrar's interests include phones, streaming, autonomous vehicles, internet trends, entertainment, pop culture and digital accessibility. In addition to her current role, she's worked for CNET's video, culture and news teams. She graduated with bachelor's and master's degrees in journalism from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. title: The Apple Pencil turned the Duo into my new favorite notebook
snippet: If not notebook, why notebook shaped? Apple's $2,000 folding phone is a surprisingly good stand-in for a $20 notebook. Believe me; nothing gets me going quite like a new notebook. This one will be different, I think. This time, I really will take it everywhere. And a few weeks, a month, or maybe a year later, I'll concede that it didn't change everything an … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Apple’s $2,000 folding phone is a surprisingly good stand-in for a $20 notebook.

Believe me; nothing gets me going quite like a new notebook. This one will be different, I think. This time, I really will take it everywhere. Inspiration can strike at any moment, and you have to be ready, says David Sedaris in that one MasterClass I watched on a flight. With this one special new notebook, I will see the world differently. I’ll steal moments for myself to write, rather than pulling out my phone to scroll at every opportunity like a trained monkey. And a few weeks, a month, or maybe a year later, I’ll concede that it didn’t change everything and add it to my notebook graveyard. At least they all look nice on the corner of my desk?

The iPhone Duo is not a notebook — although it is the first iPhone to support the Apple Pencil. Even so, I can see the new notebook effect in the eyes of the people I talk to about the Duo. “Is that the new iPhone?” the conversation starts. I hand over the phone and give them the short version of our 26-minute review: It’s nice, it’s kind of heavy and chunky, you should wait for the second generation. They nod, but I can tell they still want one anyway. They’re tired of their big/aging/boring phone, they tell me. And this one would be different.

It’s hard to argue against. It really is a different phone. Its new form factor lets you actually use it in meaningfully different ways. The Duo can act like a vintage Hasselblad with a waist-level viewfinder. It can be a book-shaped e-reader. And with this week’s iOS 27.2 update officially adding that Apple Pencil support, it can also be a notebook.

Notebooks are nice and help you express creativity. Phones are bad attention-stealing machines, or something.

That’s the USB-C Apple Pencil, to be specific, so there’s no pressure sensitivity. You do still get the ability to “scribble” handwriting that’s automatically turned into text in apps like Messages or Safari, as you can on the iPad. But even with the basic stylus, there’s a lot of fun to be had doodling and writing notes out by hand. I asked for some Pencil-friendly app suggestions and downloaded a handful. I used the native Notes app to scribble down some article ideas. I set my five-year-old loose on a blank note, to his delight (the phone survived the encounter, too). But having the stylus in my hand led me on an unexpected side quest: turning the whole phone into a notebook.

Why not? It’s notebook-shaped. Notebooks are nice and help you express creativity. Phones are bad attention-stealing machines, or something. Maybe I could cajole the Duo into being something less distracting, more input-friendly. I put together a minimalist home and lockscreen designed around this theory. I won’t lie, it’s pretty nice. But I don’t think I curated my way out of the new-notebook trap, even if it was a fun exercise.

There aren’t many apps ready to take advantage of the new stylus support. Notes, unsurprisingly, is where the Pencil is at its best. When you use the Pencil for handwriting in the app, you can enable the auto-refine handwriting feature that neatens up your writing while still keeping its unique characteristics intact. This has been available on the iPad since 2024, and it’s particularly useful on the Duo’s comparatively small screens.

It occasionally gets tripped up by some of my scrawl that it either doesn’t know what to do with or misinterprets — it kept insisting on turning a “u” into an “o” in one instance. And it works after a small delay when you pause your writing, which I can see being distracting if I really want to get into a flow state. But it’s a nice middle ground between my untidy scribbles and full handwriting-to-text conversion and very handy for something like a grocery list.

The Notes app also has a big homescreen widget that kind of turned the phone into a notebook, but wasn’t nice to look at. After some more digging, I found almost exactly what I’d been looking for: TypeDraw.

Writing on the Duo’s inner screen is pretty delightful.

It’s a $4.99 one-time purchase, and it’s optimized for the Duo. When you launch the app, it turns the cover screen into the front of your notebook. To flip to a page, you can either swipe on the cover screen or open the whole phone. It’s a delight.

TypeDraw isn’t really for power note-takers the way other apps like Bear are. You can’t add tags or links between notes, and you’re limited to one notebook. But it automatically creates a table of contents at the beginning based on the headings of your notes, so you can skip right to the section you’re looking for. Plus, if you drag your finger along the “elastic” on the cover, it’ll stretch and snap back, complete with satisfying haptics. I have zero regrets about the five bucks I spent on this app.

Using the Apple Pencil with the Duo gave me one more reason to love the matte finish on the inner screen. There’s just a bit of resistance moving the pencil across the display that feels more satisfying than the lifeless plastic-on-glass effect of writing on the cover screen. It’s not going to feel like using a Remarkable tablet or anything, but it’s nice.

The Pencil has one other neat trick — it can stick to the Duo’s hinge magnetically when the phone is closed. The pencil is longer than the phone, so it’s an awkward fit, but it’s been a handy way to carry both around the house as I relocate throughout the day.

I was only, like, 60 percent serious when I set out to turn the Duo into a notebook, but I actually liked the idea the more I got into it. Reimagining my homescreen around creating rather than consuming feels like a worthwhile cause, and I’m planning to live with it for a while to see if it inspires any changes in my phone habits. To that end, I also set up a shortcut to launch TypeDraw whenever I open the inner screen.

This is my new new minimalist homescreen.

But I think the most useful part of this exercise was examining, once again, how much stuff I really need on my homescreen. I can get most things done with a Spotlight Search or a tap in the Control Center. Siri is much more helpful now too, and it’s always lurking nearby to help out. The grid of apps I’m so used to is mostly for emotional support at this point. I didn’t need a folding phone to learn that, but it helped.

Above all, the new-notebook effect proved to be just as strong as always. The shiny new thing eventually fades into the background. You certainly don’t need a $2,000 phone to reevaluate your homescreen. You can — and I will continue to — just carry a little notebook around with your regular phone. A fun new gadget is delightful, don’t get me wrong. But don’t hang all your hopes and dreams for a new you on one of them.

Apple’s $2,000 folding phone is a surprisingly good stand-in for a $20 notebook.

Believe me; nothing gets me going quite like a new notebook. This one will be different, I think. This time, I really will take it everywhere. Inspiration can strike at any moment, and you have to be ready, says David Sedaris in that one MasterClass I watched on a flight. With this one special new notebook, I will see the world differently. I’ll steal moments for myself to write, rather than pulling out my phone to scroll at every opportunity like a trained monkey. And a few weeks, a month, or maybe a year later, I’ll concede that it didn’t change everything and add it to my notebook graveyard. At least they all look nice on the corner of my desk?

title: The touchscreen MacBook Pro is just a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen
snippet: Touch ‘em if you got ‘em. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Apple's long-awaited touchscreen MacBook Pro is finally here. I got to try this MacBook that, according to the last two Apple CEOs, shouldn't exist. The most surprising thing is how normal it is. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (what a name) has one of the nicest screens I've seen on a laptop. The current Mini LED MacBook Pros are great, but the OLED has those even inkier blacks. It also gets super bright, with incredibly rich colors and infinite contrast. Apple calls it a "reference-caliber display," which is a very Apple-y marketing term, but it walks the walk by being the first laptop display with support for Apple CMF 2026 color … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Apple’s long-awaited touchscreen MacBook Pro is finally here. I got to try this MacBook that, according to the last two Apple CEOs, shouldn’t exist. The most surprising thing is how normal it is.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (what a name) has one of the nicest screens I’ve seen on a laptop. The current Mini LED MacBook Pros are great, but the OLED has those even inkier blacks. It also gets super bright, with incredibly rich colors and infinite contrast. Apple calls it a “reference-caliber display,” which is a very Apple-y marketing term, but it walks the walk by being the first laptop display with support for Apple CMF 2026 color modes.

But Apple didn’t spend 16 years saying it wouldn’t put an OLED in a laptop. The hallmark feature — the thing Apple was never going to do until it did — was the touchscreen. How would Apple prove that touchscreens on laptops aren’t “ergonomically terrible”? What magic would it bring to this input method that makes us go, “Ah-ha! Apple took its time, but it really figured it out”?

And it’s just a touchscreen.

We’re just normal touchscreen laptops. Just innocent touchscreen laptops.

Of course, I’m glad Apple is finally doing this. There’s no harm in accommodating people’s natural urge to reach out and touch something on a screen. But there’s also no magic. You can poke and swipe at the screen. Hooray! Some UI elements in macOS 27 Golden Gate and certain apps either magnify or expand a little when you tap them. It’s cool and all, but it doesn’t exactly look like it’ll reinvent how we use laptops. (Better luck in future macOS updates, I guess?)

Over a decade ago, touchscreen laptops were supposed to be revolutionary. Microsoft gave Windows 8 a whole new touch-optimized UI. Laptops started flipping and folding and getting all weird and fun. Then, Windows 8 crashed and burned, and convertible laptops became just another product segment as opposed to redefining how a laptop looks and works. Apple waited it all out, realized no one cared that much, added a touchscreen with some minor UI improvements, and went, “Okay, enjoy macOS with some swiping.”

This demo from a pro photographer used bracketed exposures and a vibe coded app to composite the images into one interactive photo. The taps and swipes on the screen were a natural way to collage the imagery, but a mouse or trackpad works too.

It’s kind of boring, but maybe a winning move. It finally rips off the Band-Aid for Apple and sets the table for touchscreens to one day come to much more attainable laptops, like the MacBook Air and Neo. Apple still has lots of touch-based devices for people who want to prioritize that. But this is just normal now: You have a laptop with a keyboard, trackpad, and a touchable screen for whenever you want to poke at it.

It’s all very strategic, as is usually the case with Apple. But it’s hard not to wonder that it could have done more. Looking at the touchscreen settings menu, I saw that most touch gestures just map to things you can already do on the trackpad. At Apple’s event, I sat in on briefings that included professionals who recently started using the touchscreen MacBook Pro. Touching the screen wasn’t redefining their workflows or how they practice their craft — they still defaulted to keyboard and trackpad functions. The touchscreen was just a bonus. When I asked a few of them if they wished the MacBook Pro included Apple Pencil support, nearly all of them said sure, that’d be cool, too. Because the more options, the better. Apple took over a decade to come around to the touchscreen. Don’t hold your breath for Pencil support or a 360-degree hinge.

This is fine.

The new OLED and lighter chassis are just as important as the touchscreen in making the new MacBook Pro feel special. The Dynamic Island is a nice upgrade over the notch. And bringing back the illuminated Apple logo is just fun! It’s actually what got the biggest reaction from the crowd during John Ternus’ incredibly brief presentation. This new MacBook Pro looks great as a whole, but there’s more magic in that lid logo than the touchscreen.

Before the event, I wondered how Apple could make a touchscreen laptop better. And, well, it just made a touchscreen laptop.

title: IQOO’s new mid-range phone puts last year’s flagships to shame
snippet: The IQOO Neo 12 is outfitted with so many premium-level specs that you’d never know this was targeted toward an upper mid-range budget. more…
fullText:
The IQOO Neo 12 is outfitted with so many premium-level specs that you’d never know this was targeted toward an upper mid-range budget.

Companies like IQOO often surprise with specs that feel like they shouldn’t belong on relatively inexpensive phones, and the IQOO Neo 12 fits right in with that. The star of the show is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, the same one in the $1300 Galaxy S26 Ultra. That’s made even better thanks to a custom 59-blade active cooling fan and a “3D Ice Dome” vapor chamber inside.

On the front is a generous 6.83-inch 185Hz AMOLED panel with 2K resolution, a 2,200-nit peak brightness rate, and both DC dimming and 2,160Hz PWM dimming for eye comfort. Unsurprisingly, for a gaming-centric phone, it’s also got a custom display chip for IQOO 16-level touch responsiveness and a “super-sensitive gyro” for epic gyro aiming in games.

Despite having an active fan, this one features an IP69 rating, so it can be abused in all sorts of ways without seeing water or dust damage. A 9,000mAh battery is inside with support for 100W wired charging, and an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor, IR sensor, and stereo speakers round out the build.

	

The IQOO Neo 12 packs a 50MP Sony IMX921 main camera sensor alongside an 8MP ultra-wide camera in the stylish raised camera island on the back, plus a 16MP selfie up front. Phone colorway options include Contender, Frost Blade Blue, and Shadow Black. This one is making its initial debut in China for:

12GB/256GB for CNY 4,199 ($630)

12GB/512GB for CNY 4,899 ($735)

16GB/256GB for CNY 4,599 ($690)

16GB/512GB for CNY 5,299 ($825)

16GB/1TB for CNY 6,299 ($945)

Not too shabby, given the specs. Chinese users can buy it from Vivo right now. A global release date has not yet been announced.

title: Google Photos rolls out customizable redesign of your ‘Collections’ tab
snippet: Following the floating navigation bar in July, Google Photos is rolling out a big redesign that lets you customize the Collections tab on Android and iOS. more…
fullText:
Following the floating navigation bar in July, Google Photos is rolling out a big redesign that lets you customize the Collections tab on Android and iOS.

The previous design started with a 2×2 grid. Favorites and Trash were at the top, while the other two shortcuts changed based on usage. Then there were large cards for Albums, On this device, People & pets, Wardrobe, Documents, Places, Stickers, and Moments. On Android, this was followed by a list: Screenshots, Videos, Recently Added, Archive, and Locked.

Old

This redesign of Collections is focused on customization. The first section is called “Pinned” and lets you choose which cards appear. By default, the carousel shows Favorites, Screenshots, and Trash. You also have the option to remove this section entirely. 

	
	

That’s followed by carousels for On this device, Albums, People & pets, Wardrobe, Places, and Documents. “View all” at the top-right corner lets you jump straight to the full grid or list view. Other options let you hide each section and rearrange the order in which they appear.

New

The “Other Collections” grid rounds out this page: Favorites, Screenshots, Moments, Videos, Recently Added, Stickers, Creations, Archive, Locked, and Trash. The “Reorder” button is found at the very bottom. 

This redesign is now widely rolling out with Google Photos 7.97 (Android) and 7.98 (iOS). Instead of the usual Force stop on Android, we’ve curiously been able to get this server-side update by restarting our devices and then opening the Photos app.

fullText:
It’s been a busy fall for Apple. iOS and macOS 27 arrived in September, iPhone Duo went on sale just a few days ago, and more Mac announcements are expected later this week. Between the new software and hardware, there’s plenty for Apple users to explore.

Of all these announcements, the iPhone Duo has arguably attracted the most attention. As the first iPhone with a fundamentally different form factor, it introduces new possibilities for how we use our phones. But new hardware is only part of the story. Just as important is how apps take advantage of it. For an app like Craft, which brings notes, tasks, and documents together in one place, the larger display and new multitasking capabilities open up interesting new ways to work.

Craft is ready for iPhone Duo from day one, with an interface designed to take advantage of its new form factor. And while the Duo is getting much of the attention right now, Craft has also seen a steady stream of improvements across iPhone, iPad, and Mac over the past few months.

And there’s an additional bonus for anyone looking to give Craft a try: 40% off for life with code 9to5Mac40, available through this exclusive 9to5Mac offer.

From quick notes to big ideas: Craft on iPhone Duo

Craft has always been developed specifically for Apple’s platforms, with the same features available across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, but an interface tailored to each device. That approach carries over to iPhone Duo, where Craft adapts between compact and unfolded poses.

In its compact form, Craft works much like it does on any other iPhone. You can quickly capture an idea, check off a task, or work on a document with the full set of editing and formatting tools. Unfold the device, though, and there’s suddenly much more room to work with. Writing, organizing information, and navigating longer documents all benefit from the additional space. The matte inner display with its nano-texture finish is particularly well suited to reading, especially when browsing through Craft’s richly styled documents.

The larger display is also a good fit for some of Craft’s more advanced features. Collections, for example, let you organize information in structured views, including Tables and Kanban boards. Being able to see more cards and information at once makes these views considerably more useful on the unfolded screen.

One of the Duo specific iOS features that has gotten the most praise from reviewers is the new side-by-side multitasking mode, and it’s particularly useful with Craft. You can keep a document open on one side of the screen and Photos on the other, dragging images directly into your document. Or open Safari alongside Craft to drag over text, images, and even entire web pages while researching a topic or putting together a mood board.

It’s a good example of how the new form factor can make familiar workflows feel quite different, without requiring an entirely new way of using the app.

Built for the entire Apple ecosystem

For those unfamiliar with Craft, it’s a productivity app that brings notes, tasks, and documents together in one place. You can capture ideas, organize projects, plan your day, and create polished documents to share with others, all within the same app.

Craft is available on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even Apple Vision Pro, with fast syncing that makes it easy to move between devices. It’s also built to work offline, so you can keep writing or organizing your notes on the subway or during a flight. Your changes sync automatically once you’re connected again.

But Craft’s approach goes beyond making the same app available everywhere. Its interface and interactions are designed for each platform, whether you’re working with touch on an iPhone or using a keyboard and trackpad on a Mac. One of Craft’s strengths is how easy it makes it to create good-looking documents, without having to spend much time adjusting layouts or formatting. And if you want to share your work, you can turn any document into a website with a single click.

And of course, being so deeply integrated into the Apple ecosystem, Craft takes full advantage of Apple’s OS features. Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets keep frequently used content within reach, Shortcuts lets you automate common workflows, and Siri AI makes it possible to access and work with your Craft content without always having to open the app.

Craft keeps getting better, wherever you use it

While the iPhone Duo launch is a good reason to take another look at Craft, quite a bit has changed in the app itself over the past few months. Rather than focusing exclusively on adding new features, the Craft team has spent much of the summer revisiting existing ones, improving how they work and making everyday interactions faster and more consistent.

The team started by revisiting tasks. In Craft, tasks can live directly inside your notes and documents, keeping them close to the information they’re related to. At the same time, dedicated task views bring everything together, so you can see what’s due today, plan upcoming work, and keep track of tasks across different projects without having to open each document individually.

Templates have also become more flexible. You can start with one of Craft’s existing templates or create your own for recurring workflows, whether that’s meeting notes, project plans, or weekly reflections. You can now also assign a default template to your Daily Notes, so every new day starts with the structure you’ve chosen.

Another area where Craft has taken a somewhat different approach is AI. Rather than making it central to every interaction, Craft treats AI as an optional tool that users can incorporate into their workflow as much or as little as they like.

Craft Assistant is built into the app and can help with writing, editing, and working with information in your documents. You can use it through Craft’s built-in credit system or connect your own AI provider using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK). For those who prefer working with external AI tools, Craft also supports MCP, making it possible to connect your documents and tasks to other agents and build more customized workflows.

And if you’d rather not use AI at all, you can simply disable the assistant in Settings. Unlike some productivity apps that are increasingly building their entire experience around AI, Craft isn’t pushing AI into every interaction, forcing you to change how you work, or making you pay more for features you never asked for. Whether you use its built-in assistant, bring your own provider, or turn AI off entirely, the choice remains yours.

A good time to try Craft

With a new experience on iPhone Duo and a long list of improvements across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, Craft has plenty to offer both new and returning users. Whether you’re looking to organize your notes and tasks or create documents that are easy to share, there’s quite a bit worth exploring.

And there’s an additional incentive for anyone looking to give Craft a try: 40% off for life with code 9to5Mac40, available through the exclusive 9to5Mac offer.

title: Even your abuelita will love Even Realities’ new smart glasses styles
snippet: Grab a cup of hot cocoa and a sweater, because Even Realities’ new styles and glasses accessories are warming up for the fall. more…
fullText:
Grab a cup of hot cocoa and a sweater, because Even Realities’ new styles and glasses accessories are warming up for the fall.

Just in time for the first anniversary, we’re getting a brand new Even Realities G2 colorway, in addition to two new accessories that have been requested since launch.

The new Even Realities G2 colorway is simply called “Brown 2,” and uses a new material to combine the structural nature and balance of G2 glasses with the classy look of tortoiseshell frames. Brown 2 maintains all the great camera-free features of G2 smart glasses, and even ships in both Frame A and Frame B styles (that’s round or square, basically) for $649. The previous grey, brown, and green colors are also still available.

To go along with the new Even Realities G2 colorway, buyers can also select the new Even G2 Chain to keep your glasses hanging on your neck when not worn. Since Even Realities G2 weighs between 38-42 grams, depending on the style, they won’t feel heavy on your neck (or your face). G2 Chain is made of stainless steel with a sandblasted gunmetal finish and retails for $79.

	

Lastly, G2 users can now finally choose a polarized glasses clip (pictured above in Frame B style) that pops onto the frames. This is great for all-day outdoor wear since it tints the frames (and, by proxy, also makes the in-lens display easier to read in bright outdoor lighting). G2 Clip Polarized comes with a special case and retails for $149.

The new Even Realities G2 colorway and accessories come alongside a big new software update, including a new Conversate Pro mode that changes the way the glasses remember information you tell them. If you’re not familiar with the glasses, check out our Even Realities G2 review.

title: Apple’s European government affairs chief to speak at Web Summit 2026
snippet: Apple’s Director of European Government Affairs, Sébastien Gros, will speak at this year’s Web Summit in Lisbon, Portugal, taking place November 9–12. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple’s Director of European Government Affairs, Sébastien Gros, will speak at this year’s Web Summit in Lisbon, Portugal, taking place November 9–12. Here are the details.

Apple to return to Web Summit

Over the past few years, Apple has regularly sent executives to speak at Web Summit.

From Craig Federighi, who argued against allowing sideloading on the iPhone in 2021, to Sumbul Desai discussing Apple’s healthcare initiatives in 2022, to Sarah Herrlinger exploring accessibility and AI in 2024, to Apple Music co-lead Ole Obermann discussing the music industry in 2025, Apple has used the event to address a wide range of topics.

This year, as spotted by iFeed, the company will send Sébastien Gros, its Director of Government Affairs for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA), to speak at the event.

As of now, details about Gros’s participation, including the subject of his session, have not yet been announced.

As is usually the case, this year’s Web Summit is shaping up to be a massive gathering, with more than 850 speakers (including a few humanoid robots) from dozens of countries and territories, representing hundreds of companies alongside universities, public institutions and other organizations.

For those following Apple, another notable speaker on this year’s lineup is Tony Fadell, the former Apple executive who helped create the iPod and iPhone.

snippet: YouTube is rolling out, or at least testing, a new update on Google TV that makes YouTube Music stand out like a sore thumb, and I am not a fan. more…
fullText:
YouTube is rolling out, or at least testing, a new update on Google TV that makes YouTube Music stand out like a sore thumb, and I am not a fan.

YouTube’s UI on TVs changes occasionally without much warning, and its latest update is now showing up on Google TV. I’d say it’s a subtle change, but it sure doesn’t feel that way.

That’s because the YouTube Music icon along the side has been replaced with a bright red logo, the only colored icon along that sidebar. Compared to the UI seen previously (above), it really stands out.

The Music tab is unchanged here, still showing music videos and content from artists you’ve listened to or follow. 

	

This change may end up showing up beyond just Google TV, as YouTube’s TV app design is shared across multiple platforms. Personally, though, I hope this one ends up being taken back.

What do you think?

title: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86
snippet: “Captain Picard stood for the best of us,” wrote William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk.
fullText:
Patrick Stewart, the British actor whose calm demeanor and steely strength led the Star Trek television franchise into its next generation, died Wednesday at age 86. The actor suffered from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the care of his beloved wife Sunny,” a Thursday post on Stewart’s Instagram account read in part. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Through a long career, Stewart starred in everything from Shakespeare productions to superhero films, but his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation is firmly cemented in entertainment culture. Show creator Gene Roddenberry didn’t at first think Stewart, who was bald, could play the virile captain he had envisioned for the new Star Trek series. Stewart even had his wife ship his toupee over from London, and he wore it for an audition scene, but executives saw him with both styles and chose the bald look.

			

More from CNET

Patrick Stewart stands front and center with the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation. Pictured in the front row are, from left, Marina Sirtis as Counselor Deanna Troi, Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Gates McFadden as Dr. Beverly Crusher. Seen in the back row, from left, are Jonathan Frakes as Commander William Riker, Brent Spiner as Lieutenant Commander Data, Whoopi Goldberg as Guinan, LeVar Burton as Lieutenant Commander Geordi La Forge, and Michael Dorn as Lieutenant Worf.CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images

Stewart was stepping into big boots. While the original Star Trek only ran for three seasons, from 1966 to 1969, it soon became a pop culture fixture, and the success of the first Star Wars film in 1977 finally allowed Roddenberry to make feature films using his original cast. The success of those movies led to a new series, Star Trek: The Next Generation, which launched in 1987 and took place about a century after the original show.

With his resonant voice and complete command of the crew, Stewart’s Picard came off as a trained diplomat compared with the more swashbuckling Capt. James T. Kirk, as played by William Shatner on the original Star Trek. But there was no question who was in charge on his bridge, and his crew followed him unhesitatingly. That made later episodes, including the third-season plot where Picard was assimilated by the alien Borg, even more meaningful, as a very human Picard struggled to recover from what had been done to him.

Professor X and more

Star Trek: The Next Generation ran from 1987 to 1994, but Stewart wasn’t done playing leaders. He took on the role of Professor Charles Xavier, or Professor X, in the X-Men superhero franchise, playing a telepathic, wheelchair-using mutant who founded the X-Men superhero team. He portrayed Xavier in multiple films over the span of 17 years, acting alongside his longtime friend, Ian McKellen.

Ironically, McKellen originally advised Stewart not to accept the Star Trek role as Picard, reportedly telling him, “You have too much important theater work to do. You can’t throw that away to do TV.”

Stewart began his acting career on the British stage, working with the Royal Shakespeare Company and winning numerous acting awards. 

He was bluntly open about his childhood with an abusive father, writing in the Guardian newspaper in 2009 that the experience never left him.

“As a child I witnessed his repeated violence against my mother, and the terror and misery he caused was such that, if I felt I could have succeeded, I would have killed him,” Stewart wrote. “If my mother had attempted it, I would have held him down.”

Fans and friends remember

Shatner remembered his successor with tenderness and also referenced the death days earlier of Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov on the original Star Trek.

“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on X. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”

What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of…

— William Shatner (@WilliamShatner) October 29, 2026

George Takei, who played helmsman Hikaru Sulu on the original Star Trek, also remembered Stewart.

“Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before.”

Wil Wheaton, who played young Wesley Crusher on Star Trek: The Next Generation, posted a photo of the two together, with a broken heart emoji and the words, “Godspeed, Captain.”

Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny, and two children.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Gael Cooper

She's been a journalist since 1989, working at Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, Twin Cities Sidewalk, the Minneapolis Star Tribune, and NBC News Digital. She's Gen X in birthdate, word and deed. title: HomePod 27.2 hands-on: default wireless speaker for Mac, Sound Glow and more [Video]
snippet: iOS 27.2 and its corresponding updates for the HomePod lineup bring several key new features to Apple’s smart speakers. The most exciting update? The ability to finally use your HomePod as the default sound output for your Mac. This means that the 2nd-generation HomePod and HomePod mini 2 can now function as low-latency wireless speakers for your Mac! Watch our hands-on video for an in-depth look at how the new wireless speaker functionality works, along with other new features like Sound Glow, Lock Controls, and home theater surround sound support. Be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more in-depth videos. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 and its corresponding updates for the HomePod lineup bring several key new features to Apple’s smart speakers. The most exciting update? The ability to finally use your HomePod as the default sound output for your Mac. This means that the 2nd-generation HomePod and HomePod mini 2 can now function as low-latency wireless speakers for your Mac!

Watch our hands-on video for an in-depth look at how the new wireless speaker functionality works, along with other new features like Sound Glow, Lock Controls, and home theater surround sound support. Be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more in-depth videos.

HomePod as speakers for Mac

It’s long been possible to use a HomePod as a wireless speaker for the Mac, but doing so came with at least one big caveat: wireless latency. While it’s generally fine for movie playback, the latency is immediately noticeable when playing anything in real time. For example, playing instruments in Logic Pro, audio and FaceTime calls, etc. For these particular applications, HomePods have, up until now, been less than ideal speakers for the Mac.

Video walkthrough

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Apple has addressed this issue in the 27.2 update, significantly reducing latency when using a HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) as a wireless speaker for Mac desktops and laptops that support Wi-Fi 6E. This, unfortunately, excludes some early Apple Silicon machines, such as those powered by the M1 family of chips, but it’s good to see this feature made available.

HomePod 2nd Generation set as the Default System Output Device in System Profiler

For the HomePod mini 2, Apple included a different Wi-Fi/Bluetooth architecture based on PCIe and revised audio routing to prioritize low-latency applications. It’s also worth noting that Apple’s Wi-Fi 6E requirement applies to the Mac hardware itself and doesn’t imply that a user needs a 6E-enabled router.

HomePod 1 vs HomePod 2 latency test with Logic Pro

From that, we can gather that the update will allow the HomePod to work similarly to how it currently works with an Apple TV, when set as the default audio source. In other words, instead of relying on traditional AirPlay, it creates an ad hoc point-to-point connection between the Mac and the HomePod for minimal latency. This will make a HomePod a viable speaker-output destination for real-time audio applications.

Notice that the Play sound effects through setting now allows for AirPlay

Apple is so confident of the low-latency connection that it defaults to playing sound effects via AirPlay when a compatible HomePod is selected as the output destination. Obviously, sound effects are the sort of thing that relies on low latency, since their sound has to correspond to what is happening in the environment at that exact time; otherwise, it would be disorienting. If I select my HomePod mini (1st generation), that option is not even available.

The Play sound effects through setting doesn’t allow for AirPlay on older HomePod hardware

Needless to say, this update instantly has me reconsidering my speaker needs for my Mac desktop setup. I recently got rid of my Yamaha HS3s because I’m looking for something with a little more umph. A pair of full-sized 2nd-generation HomePods in a stereo pair would definitely fit the bill, and look much better to boot.

Lock Controls

Have you ever accidentally brushed the touch sensor on the top cap of the HomePod, activating it to play music? Do you have pets who surreptitiously activate your HomePod while you’re not in the room? If so, then the new Lock Controls switch in 27.2 will help.

When Lock Controls is enabled, the touch surface on top of the HomePod is locked, meaning touch, touch-and-hold, and volume adjustments are disabled. You’ll easily recognize when Lock Controls is enabled by the bright red “no” animation that appears.

Even the first-gen HomePod gets some love

Lock Controls will prevent a HomePod from playing audio or taking action when the device’s top cap is touched. However, intercom, alarms, timers, Check in, and FaceTime calls will continue to respond to touch.

Of all the new features in the 27.2 software update, Lock Controls is the only one that appears on all HomePod models, regardless of generation. That means that, yes, even the original OG HomePod lands support for the handy new addition!

Sound Glow

My favorite new feature in the 27.2 update is Sound Glow. This is the feature that displays ambient light that corresponds to the colors and rhythm of the album artwork for the music or podcasts being played.

Sound Glow takes full advantage of the LED Matrix displays beneath the HomePod top cap. The big HomePod features an array of 37 RGB LEDs, while the smaller HomePod mini features an array of 19 RGB LEDs. As a side note, the original HomePod features 19 LEDs across a smaller surface area than the updated version.

To enable Sound Glow, you must update your iOS device and your HomePod to 27.2. Once updated, open the Home app and venture into the settings for the HomePod you wish to adjust. There, you’ll find a Sound Glow switch you can enable. 

Apple notes that you’ll also be able to toggle Sound Glow with your voice, but it will require an Apple Intelligence‑enabled iPhone running the latest software. This could be enabled once Apple enables Siri AI on the HomePod mini 2, and perhaps the 2nd-generation HomePod, but this remains to be seen.

Home theater surround sound

If you plan to purchase an Apple TV 4K (fourth-generation), you’re likely interested in the new home theater surround sound option available with the HomePod mini 2 or the 2nd-generation full-sized HomePod. This feature lets you use four HomePods, two identical matching stereo pairs in front and rear, for a surround sound setup.

I haven’t been able to personally test this yet, because I don’t yet have the newest Apple TV 4K, but I can bet it will sound fantastic, especially when four full-sized Dolby Atmos-enabled HomePods are involved. That being said, this is an expensive proposition.

Here are the pricing details for those looking to set up a four-speaker home theater surround sound option:

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Four HomePod 2 ($349×4) = $1695

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Two HomePod 2 ($349×2) + two HomePod mini 2 ($149×2) = $1295

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Four HomePod mini 2 ($149×4) = $895

By way of comparison, Sonos’ Dolby Atmos-enabled four-speaker Immersive Set with Beam Ultra bundle can be had for less than $1600 and comes with a dedicated subwoofer. I’m not a home audio expert or an audiophile, so I can’t say which one is better, but it’s interesting that both it and the highest-tier HomePod surround setup are so similar in price.

When managing your HomePod speakers via the tvOS interface on the Apple TV 4K, you’ll see new options for Surround Sound and Whole Room Audio under the Home Theater section. The surround sound option is self-explanatory and ideal for movies and television shows, but the Whole Room Audio option is better suited to listening to music, as it provides left- and right-channel placement no matter which direction you face.

9to5Mac’s Take

iOS 27.2 provides noteworthy updates to all HomePod models, including the original HomePod, which now includes the new Lock Controls capability. But the real fun starts with the HomePod mini, with its Sound Glow support, and the HomePod mini 2 and HomePod 2nd-generation, with their support for working as the default speaker for Wi-Fi 6E-enabled Mac hardware. I think a pair of HomePod mini 2’s would look great sitting next to Apple’s just-released M6 iMac.

What do you think? Are you planning to get any of Apple’s new Home-focused hardware, or are you looking to take advantage of the new 27.2 features on hardware you already own? Sound off in the comments with your thoughts on the matter.

title: Apple VP talks new iPad mini: OLED without ProMotion, Acoustic Display, more
snippet: Apple unveiled its “biggest update ever” for the iPad mini this week, introducing a thinner, lighter design and an OLED display. In a pair of interviews, Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering, discussed the new iPad mini’s design, display, and more. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled its “biggest update ever” for the iPad mini this week, introducing a thinner, lighter design and an OLED display.

In a pair of interviews, Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering, discussed the new iPad mini’s design, display, and more.

While the new iPad mini features an OLED display, it doesn’t support ProMotion. Instead, it’s limited to a 60Hz refresh rate. Here’s what Pakula had to say about that decision in an interview with Chris Lawley:

Display experience is about more than just a single spec. One of the things that’s really cool about OLED is it actually has this really fast pixel response time. So it’s more than an order of magnitude faster than the pixel response time for an LCD display.

What that does is it makes everything really smooth. Motion blur is significantly reduced compared to LCD. When you pair that with the other things, the contrast, the brightness, and the color, this is just a killer display.

In addition to being lighter and thinner, the new iPad mini is also IP67-rated for water and dust resistance, a first for an iPad. One key enabler is a new Acoustic Display. Pakula explains how that technology works:

One of the cool things we realized as we started experimenting was that the unique size and form factor of this display actually had a resonant frequency that’s in the audible range.

I think more importantly, it’s in the range of like a traditional woofer that you’d have in a speaker. What we did was we built these custom drivers that actually energize the display and emit sound directly through the enclosure, but that only really works for the mid and low frequencies.

For the higher frequencies, we actually designed these little custom tweeters. There’s one on each end of the product, and they’re actually ported out through these hidden ports between the glass and the aluminum. The result is we have this product that’s water and dust resistant. I think the sound that comes from it is so surprising for a form factor of this size.

Pakula also sat down with Katarina Mogus for an interview, where he discussed how the iPad mini fits into a world where iPhone Duo also exists:

What we love about the iPad mini is it’s really the full iPad experience in the palm of your hand. That gives you access to a million+ apps in the App Store. It’s got incredibly powerful creative accessories like the Apple Pencil Pro. And it’s got the advanced multitasking of iPadOS 27. 

It is really incredibly universal. And honestly, with all these updates, all of those experiences just got so much better.

You can watch both interviews below. The new iPad mini is available to pre-order now, with the first orders arriving on November 6.

title: 140,000 Folds and Counting for the iPhone Duo in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. How High Will It Go?
snippet: We’re folding Apple’s iPhone Duo over and over — 900 times an hour — to test the durability of its hinge.
fullText:
Since Apple’s first-ever foldable phone — the iPhone Duo — launched a week ago, everyone has been examining the hinge and looking for ways to push it to its limits. We braved three hours at the Apple store to snag our own testing model for our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, where I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations.

So, the real question: How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? At 9:30 a.m. ET on Friday, Oct. 30, we passed 140,000 folds.

Our goal is simple. On Friday, my team and I loaded the Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve also already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone. 

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge. 

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience. 

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo. 

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube today from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day. 

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test. 

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Matthew Murray
						

						

							Lab Director						
					

										

								

											As lab director for the CNET Group, Matthew leads the Labs team, which helps coordinate and conduct product testing for CNET and other Ziff Davis editorial brands including PCMag and ZDNET. He previously spent eight years as head of testing at Future plc, and before that eight years as an analyst and writer at PCMag. His technology writing has also appeared in publications including Computer Shopper, ExtremeTech, Tom's Guide, Laptop and Backstage.

title: A Touchscreen MacBook Pro Just Invites More Filthy Fingerprints
snippet: Commentary: Yes, I’m judgy about how smudgy Apple’s new laptop screen is going to be.
fullText:
I had to suppress a shudder at the thought of how smudgy the touchscreen display on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is going to get. Unlike every other Apple laptop, you can directly tap and swipe on this new MacBook Pro screen like an iPad or iPhone. I try to rarely even brush the screen of my laptop, and yet it still ends up with its share of oily smudges.

To be clear: It’s not like I’m reaching into a bucket of greasy fried chicken when typing away at my MacBook Pro. But even with normal use, skin oils build up on the keyboard. Shutting the laptop brings those oily keys directly into contact with the glass, stamping the display with a ghostly grid of gunk.

Ages ago, I would slip a microfiber cloth between the screen and keyboard whenever I shut my laptop, but I eventually gave that up. Now, I regularly wipe it down with a screen-cleaning spray called Whoosh, recommended to me by an Apple Store employee.

			

More from CNET

The new MacBook Pro gets the same oleophobic coating, a surface treatment meant to minimize fingerprints, as found on iPad, iPhone and the announced HomeView. We’ll have to see if it’s any more or less successful on the large PROLED XDR display when we test it out.

The least Apple could have done was include its $9 Polishing Cloth for free, but the cloth remains a separate accessory purchase.

A touchscreen Apple laptop has been inevitable since the first iPad — heck, even the first iPhone — which has trained a generation that screens are meant to be tapped, swiped and pinched. Apple even tested a laptop touch interface with the Touch Bar on MacBook Pros for several years before finally giving up. People I love and respect nonetheless send a shiver down my spine when they stab their laptop screen — or worse, touch my screen — to point out something.

I’ll take the MacBook Pro’s Touch Bar over a touch screen.

Sarah Tew/CNET

Am I oversensitive to fingerprints on a screen? Most definitely. But I know I’m not the only one.

As a photographer, I want to see my photos on the best possible screen, and this one is certainly Apple’s premium laptop display. Because it’s OLED, the blacks should be truly black, and colors look extremely vibrant. Apple says its 2,000-nit brightness makes it easy to use in bright light, and it has a wider color gamut that covers both P3 and Adobe RGB color spaces.

But I also want to know that when I’m using software to remove errant dust spots from my images, I’m not clicking the same area four times because the spot is actually a smudge on the glass.

So. Much. Screen. Contact. (And are musicians really going to reach for the screen like this? I’m skeptical.)Apple

Could I buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR and never touch the screen? Probably. But that feels like paying extra for a feature I wouldn’t use, even though the improvements are rolled in. You can’t get the OLED quality without the touchscreen.

And making it a touchscreen display invites more skin-to-glass contact. The question is whether I’d be able to keep my paws off the screen when I just want to zoom in on a map or dismiss a notification.

For the time being, a touchscreen Mac isn’t high on my list of features. But as I type this, I am realizing my display is once again in serious need of a good cleaning.

title: These 7 iPhone Duo-Ready Apps Make the Most of Apple’s New Foldable Phone
snippet: Several creative apps are already optimized to take advantage of the iPhone Duo’s many display configurations, with more to come.
fullText:
In addition to giving the iPhone line a new design, the iPhone Duo lets developers take advantage of several new modes to play with. But a week into the iPhone Duo’s general release, apps are still catching up to what Apple’s foldable phone can do.

The shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos. Some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker. 

		

			

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s gotten an iPhone Duo (or it’s coming soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested. 

1. Netflix

Netflix on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent. 

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

2. NYT Cooking

NYT Cooking on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

3. Fantastical

Fantastical on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

4. Edits by Instagram

Edits on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

5 and 6. TikTok and Instagram

Instagram on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

7. Toastie

Toastie on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster. 

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

There are many ways to pair up apps on the iPhone Duo for your convenience.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Bonus: Your duo of choice

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-size phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other. 

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Kerry Wan
						

						

							Contributor						
					

											

								

											Kerry Wan is the former Editor-in-Chief of ZDNET, based in New York City.
He has over 10 years of experience testing and reviewing consumer technology from mobile hardware to home entertainment.

title: Gemini Notebook for Android, iOS adds built-in audio recorder
snippet: After introducing Connected App integration last week, Gemini Notebook has rolled out an audio recorder on Android and iOS. more…
fullText:
After introducing Connected App integration last week, Gemini Notebook has rolled out an audio recorder on Android and iOS.

Between the camera and “Create New” floating action button at the bottom, you’ll see a new microphone icon. This lets you “capture lectures and record your thoughts on the go,” with the audio file creating a new notebook if you launch the recorder from the homepage. 

Your notes will live directly alongside your sources, meaning you can chat, cite, and build from them anytime, all while making ongoing edits. 

Recordings will be saved to an existing Notebook if you tap the microphone from the Sources tab.

The recorder interface is very simple with a pause button and checkmark that starts the upload once you’re done. A Gemini Notebook-themed waveform and live count appear above. You can switch to another application or lock your screen and have recordings continue in the background. There’s a 1-hour capture limit.

	

Google first announced the audio recorder in September, and it’s now widely rolling out today on Android and iOS. Force stop the app if it’s not live on your device.

Meanwhile, Google this week made a small tweak wherein tapping the “Create New” FAB immediately starts a new notebook rather than sliding up the “Add a source” panel. 

These updates follow the recent launch of the Live button in the Chat tab that lets you have a real-time conversation with your notebooks.

fullText:

Back in May 2026, Google announced that video apps on Android Auto would be available this year on select vehicles. This would support using your car’s display for watching content from apps such as YouTube, with Google also confirming that background play would kick in after the vehicle shifts out of park. 

With only two months left until Google’s year-end deadline lands, one might expect a beta release or some news on timing, but the company’s latest update doesn’t really bring much to the table.

At the Android Dev Summit this week, Google says that video and browser apps for Android Auto are still “coming soon.” Video apps are now “open” on Android Automotive (Google built-in) with browser apps in beta, but the phone-projected platform is still waiting. Google is also currently testing an updated version of audio apps using the Cars App Library, as well as new messaging and calling apps.
